📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

According to recent reports, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

In a recent development, this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most notable restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

In a recent development, we patch this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

In a recent development, new to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he released Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he rolled out Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

According to recent reports, as Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

In a recent development, eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Sources indicate that ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the newly introduced template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

Recent findings suggest that these days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Industry observers note that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

Industry observers note that this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

Recent findings suggest that the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The fresh online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Latest York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Recent findings suggest that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

According to recent reports, while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most crucial British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

According to recent reports, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

Recent findings suggest that for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy newly introduced surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Sources indicate that together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a massive group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

Industry observers note that this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

Industry observers note that in his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

In a recent development, bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in upcoming-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

In a recent development, possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

It has been revealed that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Tech Report: Your Personality May Be Partly Written in Your DNA, Massive Study of 1 Million People Reveals

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.
  • Could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others?
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.

Could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others? A large international study suggests that some of the personality traits that make us who we are may be partly rooted in our genes, raising a fascinating question about how much of our personality is determined before we are even born.

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people. Published in the journal Nature, the findings offer new insight into how genetics contributes to differences in personality, while also showing why DNA alone cannot explain who we become.

The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99.9% identical. Differences in the remaining 0.1% help influence characteristics such as appearance, disease risk, and responses to medication. The upcoming research suggests that these small genetic differences are also associated with five major dimensions of personality: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.

Scientists have known for decades that both genetics and life experiences influence personality. Finding the specific genetic differences involved has been much more difficult because personality is shaped by many genes, each contributing an extremely small effect. Detecting those subtle patterns requires enormous amounts of data.

Between 2021 and 2022, the Estonian Biobank gathered personality information from nearly 80,000 participants. Although substantial for Estonia, that sample was not large enough to reliably identify many of the genetic associations researchers were looking for.

In a recent development, the University of Tartu team therefore combined its findings with 45 other international datasets, creating a more geographically diverse study population. For certain personality traits, the researchers could analyze data from as many as 1.1 million people. The Estonian sample was the third-largest of all participating groups and used the most comprehensive personality questionnaire.

The genetic associations were remarkably consistent across different populations, including people of varying ages and geographical backgrounds. However, the identified variants explained only about 4.8% to 9.3% of the differences in personality traits.

That relatively small proportion highlights how much remains unexplained. Social relationships, environmental influences, and personal experiences may all play substantial roles, along with the ways these factors interact with a person’s genetic makeup.

One particularly interesting feature of the Estonian research allowed scientists to examine personality from two perspectives. Participants could evaluate their own personalities and invite someone who knew them to provide an independent assessment.

“No other biobank in the world offers such an opportunity!” said Uku Vainik, Professor of Behavioral Genetics at the University of Tartu.

According to recent reports, this approach helped researchers address an important question about personality research. Are genetic associations connected to characteristics that other people can actually observe, or do they mainly reflect how individuals think about themselves?

The researchers found substantial overlap between the genetic signals associated with self-reported personality traits and those identified through assessments by acquaintances.

“This shows that measurable personality traits are truly real, publicly observable characteristics of people, rather than merely individuals’ own opinions about themselves,” explained René Mõttus, Professor of Personality Psychology and co-lead of the study.

The findings are also opening upcoming avenues for understanding the relationship between personality and physical health.

In a recent development, kerli Ilves, a junior research fellow, is investigating whether personality traits may have causal connections to health-related behaviors, including those associated with body weight, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Her preliminary findings suggest that personality could influence these behaviors, although the relationship may also work in the opposite direction.

Established behavioral patterns might themselves contribute to changes in personality over time.

“We especially see this kind of relationship in smoking,” Ilves noted.

It has been revealed that researchers emphasize that these early findings do not yet establish cause and effect. Understanding whether personality shapes health habits, whether those habits alter personality, or whether both processes occur will require additional research.

“The next step is to use other methods, such as longitudinal studies, to determine whether changes in personality are accompanied by changes in health behavior, and vice versa,” explained Vainik.

The Estonian Biobank is planning another study focused on personality and cognitive functioning. By examining how personality develops and interacts with everyday behavior, researchers hope to better understand what influences people’s health choices and eventually support more effective, personalized approaches to healthy living.

Industry News: Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that.
  • Mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once.
  • In a recent development, the proposal starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any looks to release it in a paid journal as part of the âOpen Scienceâ policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details âMars Seedâ - a new architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

Mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once. One of the most notable is weight. According to the paper, the entire system weighs in at 20 metric tons - well below the threshold of Martian payloads for Starship or NASAâs proposed 25 ton Mars landers. And crucially, rather than relying on sugar or chemical inputs from Earth, the entire system wonât need any further input from our home planet once it is established on the Red one.

In a recent development, the proposal starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits. Immediately after landing, an autonomous rover sets about unloading the packageâs hardware and assembling a 40kW nuclear fission reactor modeled on the compact nuclear reactors NASA is already developing for Mars and Moon missions. About a month later, the reactor should be fully up and running, providing both electricity and âwasteâ heat that can be used to climate control a habitat.

Fraser interviews Dr. Congrui Jin about using bioreactors to grow Martian habitats.

Or in the case of this particular mission structure, to melt some ice. The system would put the heat from the nuclear reactor into a Rodriguez well - a type of ice-drilling technique that melts a pocket of underground ice and pumps the liquid water to the surface, which has already been proven in Antarctica.

It has been revealed that water is a crucial component in the entire systemâs operation. Once the first supply of it has been obtained from the âRodwellâ as itâs known, the system uses a scaled-up version of the urine-recycling system currently in place on the International Space Station (ISS) to recover around 90 percent of the water from each production batch of material.

But water isnât the only component input from Mars itself - another is dirt, or âregolithâ in the language of space exploration. The paper estimates the system will require around four tons of Martian soil deposited into its hoppers every day. This could be collected by autonomous mining machines, like NASAâs RASSOR. Approximately 800 kg of that dirt is then stirred into water-filled mixing tanks to dissolve out nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen. But that still leaves the most deadly component of Martian soil - perchlorates.

In a recent development, fraser interviews Dr. Michael Hecht, one of the main scientists behind the MOXIE experiment to create oxygen out of the atmosphere of Mars.

It has been revealed that while these would kill a normal microorganism, Pioneer Labsâ speciality is designing biological systems for use in space exploration. So they simply evolved a hardy strain of the bacterium Cupriavidus necator, which they call sPL.001, which can thrive in the equivalent of a perchlorate-laced broth of Martian regolith simulant back on Earth. That bacterium is also the key engine in creating the bioplastics that are used to 3D print the radiation-shielded habitats.

Recent findings suggest that bacteria need food though, and shipping it from Earth would be prohibitively expensive. So thereâs one final input to the system from the Red Planet - its atmosphere. The first step in that process is an upgraded version of the MOXIE experiment that successfully revealed an ability to split the carbon dioxide in Marsâ atmosphere into carbon monoxide and oxygen.

It has been revealed that typically, that system simply gets rid of the carbon monoxide to capture the oxygen for use in rocket fuel. But in Mars Seed, carbon monoxide is actually the prize. Using a technique inspired by an emerging field called âelectro-agriculture,â the system combines waste carbon monoxide gas with water to produce liquid acetic acid - the main ingredient in vinegar.

Fraser talks in detail about what we can find to live off of when we eventually do send humans to the Red Planet.

Recent findings suggest that while a diet of straight vinegar might not sound appealing to a human, to a microbe it's nourishing enough. In four separate 1,000L fermentation tanks, the engineered microbes eat this vinegar, combined with oxygen, packing themselves with a bioplastic called polyhydroxybutyrate, with the polymer eventually making up 70% of their body weight. At that point, a high-speed centrifuge harvests the bacteria cells from the liquid broth, and the resulting paste is split into two separate assembly lines.

Sources indicate that half of the raw paste is mixed with Martian dirt and fed into a giant gantry 3D printer, which then extrudes a corrugated, arched outer protective shell. Rovers then work to pile around 2m of dirt onto the outer shell, creating a barrier to the cosmic rays and micrometeorites that plague the Martian surface.

Industry observers note that the other half of the bacteria is subjected to a pressure bath of liquid carbon dioxide, again pulled straight from the atmosphere. This extracts the pure bioplastic, which is then melted and spun into an airtight, reinforced inner tent that is capable of holding a breathable atmosphere.

It has been revealed that interview with Dr. Erika DeBenedictis, the founder of Pioneer Labs. Credit - The Fresh Biology YouTube Channel.

So, in essence, this 20 ton system can be dropped on Mars, including a pair of helping rovers, and extract all of the necessary components to continually and consistently build atmosphere-tight, safe shelter for astronauts, at a rate of about 75 sq meters every 130 days. The paper notes that, comparing the system to directly launching 20 tons of pre-made plastic building materials from Earth, the break-even point of the stand-alone biofabrication facility is around 1,400 Martian days - which lines up nicely with the two orbital alignment cycles NASA is planning to utilize before sending human crews.

It has been revealed that the main difference is that the biofabrication facility never stops producing those safe habitats, which clearly is a major advantage. Despite its promise, though, there are still plenty of engineering challenges to overcome before this system will be anywhere near launch ready. But, when that time comes, it appears that we might be able to literally grow safe habitats out of Martian water, air, and soil. And that is something any future mission planner will be thrilled to have as an option.

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR).

In a recent development, this navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

Sources indicate that with this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM).

This triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each upcoming model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

Sources indicate that A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

Recent findings suggest that A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for big homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Recent findings suggest that beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

In a recent development, the most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

In a recent development, throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Sources indicate that look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Industry observers note that most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

Sources indicate that when set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

It has been revealed that for homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Industry observers note that most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is scheduled to be released in 2035.
  • GWs are ripples in spacetime that are the signatures of mergers between massive objects, either compact binaries containing stellar mass black holes, white dwarfs, and neutron stars, or between supermassive black holes (SMBH).
  • It has been revealed that by detecting GWs from SMBH mergers, scientists study how galaxies merged and grew so massive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is scheduled to be released in 2035. The ESA is still developing the mission, but it's basic design is established. It will feature three separate spacecraft flying in an equilateral triangle formation. They'll be connected by laser interfometry, and LISA will use that interferometry to detect gravitational waves (GW).

GWs are ripples in spacetime that are the signatures of mergers between massive objects, either compact binaries containing stellar mass black holes, white dwarfs, and neutron stars, or between supermassive black holes (SMBH). Astronomy is concerned with light in all its wavelengths, but gravitational waves open another window on the Universe.

It has been revealed that by detecting GWs from SMBH mergers, scientists study how galaxies merged and grew so massive. GWs from mergers between compact binaries can act as distance markers, helping cosmologists measure the expansion of the Universe. And the Universe was opaque to light in its first 380,000 years, so that time period is behind a curtain. But that curtain of opacity can't stop gravitational waves, so they can potentially bring those crucial years of the Universe's evolution into view.

But now researchers are saying that LISA may also be able to detect exoplanets.

Recent findings suggest that this artist's impression demonstrates gravitational waves from the merger of two compact objects. The presence of an exoplanet can leave a signature on these waves that LISA can detect. Image credit: NASA.

Recent findings suggest that âThe most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,â stated Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland and NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center. âIf an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way weâll be able to uncover.â.

Two new papers outline LISA's planet-detection potential, and McGrath is involved in both. He's the sole author of "Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method," published in The Astrophysical Journal. It explains how LISA could detect exoplanets.

"Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a new method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes," McGrath writes in the first paper.

It has been revealed that the GWRV operates on the same principle as the RV exoplanet detection method does. In those instances, astronomers measure the tiny wobble a star experiences as an orbiting exoplanet tugs on it. Stars rotate, and the visible part of the star rotating toward the observer is blue-shifted, while the visible part of the star rotating away is red-shifted. The wobble creates doppler shifts in the red and blue light that astronomers measure with spectrographs.

In GWRV, an orbiting exoplanet creates a wobble in the center of mass of a compact binary. That creates a detectable doppler shift in the gravitational waves instead of in starlight. The method is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period planets than traditional RV, which more readily detects massive planets on short-period orbits around lower-mass stars like M dwarfs.

Recent findings suggest that if the method works, it has some advantages over other exoplanet detection methods. "For one, GW observatories have potentially much farther reach into the Milky Way and beyond, since the GW amplitude is inversely proportional to the source distance," explains McGrath. "They will also inherently be probing post-main-sequence stellar systems, where EM observatories simply have not found as many exoplanets.".

It has been revealed that exoplanets that go undetected in compact binaries can also cloud the GW signal. That can create misunderstandings as researchers try to understand and constrain the GWs. So detecting them also clarifies the GW signal from the compact binary.

Recent findings suggest that this graphic indicates how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237 This graphic shows how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237.

It has been revealed that this work is just an initial attempt to understand how it could all work. There's much more work to be done, as McGrath himself acknowledges. For one thing, the movement of LISA itself introduces some Doppler effect into the signal that has to be managed. Ground-based GW observatories don't move, and LISA will be the first one that does.

"Future, more complex and robust analyses will be needed to better understand the ability to detect exoplanets in GW signals," McGrath writes. "But hopefully this work can better shed light on the fundamental physics that can inform those studies.".

Recent findings suggest that if LISA does detect a signal in a GW that indicates a possible exoplanet, it will only be a candidate. That signal will have to be confirmed, and that will require observations in the electromagnetic regime. That's the subject of a second paper.

McGrath is also the lead author on another paper in the same journal that focuses on validating GW exoplanet candidates. It's titled "Multimessenger Exoplanets: Combining Infrared Excess and Astrometry with Gravitational-wave Detections of Double White Dwarf Exoplanets." It explains how the JWST can confirm GW exoplanet detections, possibly with help from Gaia or the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

âBy themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency," said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the second paper. "Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.â.

LISA will see these as signals that bracket the primary GW signal from the DWD. These secondary signals are positioned in frequencies above and below the primary. So while the primary signal carries information about the DWD, the secondaries carry information about the exoplanet.

Every observatory, whether electromagnetic or gravitational, is built to detect signals at particular frequencies. LISA's frequency range means it will excel at detecting DWDs with short orbital periods. White dwarfs aren't rare, since they're the main evolutionary outcome for stars like the Sun, once they leave the main sequence. DWDs are rarer than single WDs, but astronomers still think that there are about 10 million DWDs with orbital periods of less than one hour in the Milky Way. Of those 10 million, researchers expect LISA to find about 10,000.

According to recent reports, astronomers think that LISA will find about 10,000 white dwarf doubles (DWDs) with short orbital periods. LISA should be able to detect exoplanets in DWDs, if they're there. Image Credit: Tod Strohmayer (GSFC), CXC, NASA, Illustration: Dana Berry (CXC).

LISA should be able to find the bracketed signals that exoplanets on circumbinary orbits around DWDs display. They would be candidates at first, and if those signals can be confirmed, they would be the first of those exoplanet types to be found.

Sources indicate that "This population is unique: no such planets are at the moment known around DWDs, and only a handful of circumbinary planets around main-sequence stars and planets orbiting white dwarfs (WDs) have been identified," the authors write. "Independent EM confirmation will be essential, especially for the first GW-detected exoplanets, to validate this method.".

Validation is critical, and it'll rely on electromagnetic confirmation. In their work, they use a representive known DWD (ZTF J2243+5242) to compute its detectability by LISA GWRV. "We then demonstrate two complementary EM techniquesâJWST infrared (IR) excess and Gaia or Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometryâthat could independently confirm a GW-detected planet in this fiducial system," the authors write.

An exoplanet orbiting a DWD produces more infrared than the stars themselves. The JWST is all about detecting infrared light, and it should have no problem detecting infrared excess out to a distance of about 500 light years. In their test case for a DWD at that distance, the JWST can detect an exoplanet with about five Jupiter masses, while LISA could detect one much smaller, with as little as 0.5 Jupiter masses, under perfect conditions.

It has been revealed that âOnce LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,â mentioned Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. âThese joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.â.

Recent findings suggest that the authors say we're about to enter a upcoming phase of exoplanet detections once LISA is operational. The JWST's initial planned mission was for 5 to 10 years, but it may last 20. If it does, then it will overlap with LISA for several years, and it can be used to validate LISA exoplanet detections.

"A multimessenger exoplanet would be a historic discovery, and a DWD circumbinary would help to provide key insights into planetary and stellar evolution and into a part of the exoplanet census not yet probed," the authors write.

According to recent reports, when the first gravitational wave was directly detected by LIGO/VIRGO in 2015, astronomers declared that a fresh window into the cosmos had been opened. LISA is prying that window open wider than ever, and as this work reveals, the view might be even more detailed than thought. If it can detect exoplanets beyond the scope of traditional methods, then it'll give astronomers an even more expansive view of the cosmos than they anticipated.

Scientists Discover That Young Chimpanzees May Develop Accents Just Like Humans

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.
  • Young chimpanzees may develop something resembling regional accents, with the sounds they make becoming increasingly different depending on the community in which they grow up.
  • In a recent development, much like people who pick up subtle differences in speech from those around them, chimpanzees appear to develop population-specific vocal patterns as they mature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.

Young chimpanzees may develop something resembling regional accents, with the sounds they make becoming increasingly different depending on the community in which they grow up.

In a recent development, much like people who pick up subtle differences in speech from those around them, chimpanzees appear to develop population-specific vocal patterns as they mature. The finding challenges the long-held belief that their calls are largely fixed by genetics from birth.

A research team led by doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian from the School of Biological and Behavioural Sciences at Queen Mary University of London, in collaboration with the University of Portsmouth, compared the vocalizations of infant and juvenile chimpanzees from two geographically separated populations. By examining grunts, whimpers, and laughter, the researchers found that differences between the groups became more pronounced as the animals grew older.

Not all of these differences appeared at the same time. Some population-specific vocal characteristics were already detectable during infancy, while others emerged as the chimpanzees entered their juvenile years. This provides the first evidence that differences in chimpanzee vocalizations become increasingly distinct throughout early development.

“Understanding how communication develops during early life is fundamental to understanding animal behavior. Our findings show that chimpanzee vocalizations are not simply fixed from birth but continue to develop as young animals interact with their social and ecological environments,” notes doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian.

It has been revealed that social interactions, environmental conditions, and other influences beyond genetics may therefore help shape how young chimpanzees communicate. Although the research does not establish precisely how these factors contribute to vocal development, the findings suggest that inherited traits alone cannot explain the differences between populations.

The discovery does not mean chimpanzees possess language or human-like speech, which involves an agreed vocabulary and grammar. Instead, it offers a newly introduced perspective on how communication develops in primates and how vocal patterns can differ between animal communities.

By examining communication at different stages of early life rather than simply comparing adults from different populations, the research provides a framework for investigating how communication systems emerge and diversify. It could also help scientists better understand the biological and environmental influences that shape vocal behavior across other species and the evolution of increasingly complex communication systems.

Reference: “Ontogeny of dialects across chimpanzee vocalisations” by Kassandra Giragosian, Marina Davila-Ross and Derry Taylor, 2 September 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0355313.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

It has been revealed that rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie noted his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

Recent findings suggest that “They could be a hero if they sign it,” he noted, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

According to recent reports, the petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie noted he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The latest bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Recent findings suggest that now that the newly introduced petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

According to recent reports, allies of the concern in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

Sources indicate that “Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie remarked. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that this solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind âsolar sailingâ, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a latest paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

That technology is liquid crystals, most commonly used in liquid crystal displays (LCDs). Instead of having the sail itself act like a giant mirror and requiring it to angle itself in order to turn relative to the Sun, the sail described by the RIT researchers bends sunlight at a steep angle via diffraction, allowing the spacecraft to steer sideways while still facing directly at the Sun.

Industry observers note that this solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails. The best analogy to describe how is to think of holding an umbrella against a stiff breeze. If you hold the umbrella directly facing the direction of the wind, it will push you straight back â simple enough. But, if you want to âturnâ compared to the direction of the wind, you have to angle the umbrella. In so doing, you not only lower the total amount of wind hitting the umbrella, but also make it much harder to control.

Fraser talks about how critical folding of solar sails is to their operation.

Industry observers note that traditional solar sails face the exact same problem, only in space instead of in an atmosphere and with sunlight instead of wind. Nearly a decade ago, Grover Swartzlander Jr, one of the paperâs authors and a professor at RIT, realized that microscopic optical patterns that reflected light to the side would replace mechanical tilting in solar sails. To prove his point, he received backing from NASAâs Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program, and laid out the groundwork for what became diffractive solar sails.

It has been revealed that when light hits a diffraction grating, the technical term for the microscopic patterns embedded in the sail similar to what is etched onto a CD, it bounces off at steep, predictable angles even when the surface is facing the Sun head-on. Pushing the light to one side provides the sail with an equal and opposite kick in the other direction, steering the spacecraft using nothing more than a simple roll.

While much of the early work on diffractive sail prototypes focused on patterns etched into metal-coated films, they struggled with scaling and had a hard time rolling into a rocket fairing. Hence the turn to LCDs. The new study, where the RIT team -drawing on technical input from BEAM engineering and diffractive-sail researchers at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.

Fraser talks about how great solar sails are for travel in the solar system and beyond.

Sources indicate that these flexible plastics contain rod-shaped molecules that naturally twist into microscopic spirals, creating layers of differing refractive indices that bend light using a phenomenon called the Pancharatnam phase. This is a way of bending or delaying light by twisting the direction the waves wiggle (its âpolarizationâ). Sails made out of this material have the added advantage of being lightweight, flexible, and easy to scale up manufacturing while still being able to fit inside a compact spacecraft.

Thereâs only one problem - a single liquid crystal layer only interacts with a very specific wavelength of light, allowing the rest to pass through unimpeded, and taking all their pushing power with them. To figure out how to solve this problem, the researchers turned to computer simulations, eventually using an optimization algorithm to design a three-layer sandwich of liquid crystals. The top layer catches blue and visible light, the middle layer grabs infrared, and the bottom layer interacts only with longer infrared rays. Even with those three separate layers, the combined film is only 5.5 micrometers thick, one-tenth the width of a human hair.

Sources indicate that such a setup would offer a major advantage in one potential use for a massive solar sail - as a âplanetary sunshadeâ. Scientists have long proposed parking a giant sheet in orbit at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point to deflect a small fraction of the sunlight reaching the planet, in an effort to intentionally cool it. With traditional materials, such a shade would need to tilt in order to keep its position, consequently shrinking its shadow. But one made out of diffractive material could hold its position without compromising its size. And with the latest chiral liquid crystal setup, if the middle layer is left out, the near-infrared wavelengths used by solar panels to generate electricity would still pass through - or the layers could be tuned to let the red light needed for plant photosynthesis pass through - while the rest of the sunlight still pushes on the sail.

Fraser talks about what a solar sail actually is.

In a recent development, all that being said, this concept is still at a very early stage. They havenât yet built a prototype of the three-layer system, let alone one that could stand the rigors of launch or the constant bombardment of the solar wind. But the paper offers a step to a potential solution to one of the most fundamental problems in solar sail design - and given the major advantages it has as a propulsion system, itâs only a matter of time before someone trials this fresh idea in the vacuum of space.
