Breaking: A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technology older than the laser is finding latest life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.
  • A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technology older than the laser is finding latest life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

It has been revealed that researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

Recent findings suggest that in superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

Sources indicate that that is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

According to recent reports, existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

Sources indicate that another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

“Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them newly introduced life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”.

Industry observers note that to put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

It has been revealed that in testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

In a recent development, the device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

Although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also important in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

Industry observers note that reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7.

A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity.
  • The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.
  • In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given starâs initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Sources indicate that biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across âspaceâ by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and âtimeâ by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, claims Biddle.

In a recent development, some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We donât see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

Recent findings suggest that by âstellar misalignment,â Biddle means that the starâs spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the starâs equator lies in the same plane as the planetâs orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

It is misaligned when the starâs spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a starâs tilt and the orbitâs tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

Recent findings suggest that we deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

Sources indicate that this artist's conception demonstrates a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL.

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, claims Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets.

Sources indicate that but prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, states Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar systemâs planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sunâs spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, claims Biddle.

Biddle doesnât know for certain if the Sunâs axis was tilted from the start.

But if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, says Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

Industry observers note that there isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

He is the author of the 2001 book "Distant Wanderers: The Search for Planets beyond the Solar System." He was also the host of the "Cosmic Controversy" podcast which is still available via Podbean.

Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

In a recent development, colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

In a recent development, that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Sources indicate that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Industry observers note that colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

In a recent development, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer remarked last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

According to recent reports, “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I stated, ‘You got to run,’” the Newly introduced York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Upcoming Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

It has been revealed that colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” claims a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

It has been revealed that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

📖 0% read

  • A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips.

Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

In a recent development, then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a substantial baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

According to recent reports, those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling.

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World.

It has been revealed that “I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the substantial stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen.

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking.

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash.

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most notable one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

Sources indicate that “Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World.

Industry observers note that “We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya.

Tech Report: This Common Vitamin Deficiency Could Be Quietly Disrupting Your Sleep

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.
  • Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
  • Sources indicate that the findings suggest that vitamin D may be an vital factor in sleep health as people age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.

Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with an even greater reduction in sleep duration.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that vitamin D may be an vital factor in sleep health as people age. However, the researchers caution that the study cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D levels directly improves sleep.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” says study senior author Adam Spira, PhD, MA, professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School and a core faculty member of the Johns Hopkins Center on Aging and Health.

According to recent reports, the researchers, working in collaboration with scientists at the National Institute on Aging, analyzed data from 460 men and women with an average age of approximately 71. Participants were assessed between 2012 and 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Blood samples provided measurements of vitamin D concentrations, while wrist-worn actigraphs recorded sleep and wake patterns.

After accounting for age, race, sex, and other potentially influential factors, the researchers found significant associations between higher vitamin D concentrations, longer sleep duration, and less prolonged nighttime awakenings.

When participants were classified according to clinical definitions of vitamin D deficiency, insufficiency, and normal levels, those with a deficiency slept approximately 23 minutes less than those with normal levels.

Both vitamin D deficiency and disrupted sleep are widespread among older adults. Poor sleep has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions. Earlier studies have also linked low vitamin D levels to poorer sleep quality, although clinical trials investigating the benefits of supplementation have generally involved small and relatively homogeneous populations.

In the upcoming study, the associations between vitamin D concentrations and sleep appeared strongest among Black participants.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” says study first author Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Bloomberg School’s Department of Epidemiology.

In a recent development, the team also investigated vitamin B12, which previous research has suggested may influence sleep. Women with higher B12 concentrations tended to spend less time awake after initially falling asleep. Among men, higher concentrations appeared to be associated with more nighttime wakefulness. Neither pattern was supported by conclusive statistical evidence.

The researchers could not determine whether participants obtained their vitamin D primarily through sunlight exposure, food, or supplements. Future investigations could examine whether these different sources influence sleep differently.

The study used a serial cross-sectional design, meaning that researchers analyzed a series of snapshots over time rather than establishing how changes in vitamin D levels affect subsequent sleep patterns.

Further research, particularly larger clinical trials and studies tracking changes in vitamin D and sleep over extended periods, will be needed to determine whether correcting a deficiency can meaningfully improve sleep in older adults.

Industry observers note that reference: “Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults” by Diefei Chen, Jill A Rabinowitz, Fan Wu, Zhikui Wei, Yang An, Jennifer A Schrack, Toshiko Tanaka, Chee W Chia, Mark N Wu, Sarah K Wanigatunga, Luigi Ferrucci, Eleanor M Simonsick and Adam P Spira, 14 October 2026, The Journals of Gerontology: Series A. DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212.

Support for the research was provided by the National Institute on Aging (T32AG000247, R01AG050507, HHSN-260-2004-00012C).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

At some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea. It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

In a recent development, if you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of fresh hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

In a recent development, for our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this big purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

We chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

It has been revealed that we pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

According to recent reports, in a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

Industry observers note that we like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

According to recent reports, there are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

It has been revealed that our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

We have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Sources indicate that inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

In a recent development, with 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

We like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

Sources indicate that we do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the issues folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

In a recent development, even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many users say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

It has been revealed that if aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

It’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

Sources indicate that if you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up quickly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

The full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

While Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub indicates it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

According to recent reports, the DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

There are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

Industry observers note that “The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” notes Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

He notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he indicates. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”.

It has been revealed that plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

They’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

The trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Industry observers note that hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

Sources indicate that most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

Sources indicate that if you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

It’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a substantial difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Sources indicate that courter stated that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he indicates. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”.

When it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

According to recent reports, while hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”.

Industry observers note that when it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” notes Courter.

According to recent reports, other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” indicates Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

This is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

Recent findings suggest that “As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” claims Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being stated, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

Recent findings suggest that “If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” indicates Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves.
  • First, letâs take a second to appreciate the leaps and bounds researchers have made passing data over space laser links recently.
  • Recent findings suggest that those conditions matter for an optical ground station.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit â traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev â best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sunâs gravity into a giant telescope â the raw speed of laser communication isnât the bottleneck, itâs the systemâs reliability.

First, letâs take a second to appreciate the leaps and bounds researchers have made passing data over space laser links recently. Perhaps the most impressive mission was a NASA demonstration called TBIRD, which beamed an astonishing 200 gigabits per second (Gb/s) from orbit, and completed a data transfer of five terabytes in a single five-minute pass over its receiving telescope. That is an astonishing speed for laser communication, but it had the advantage of near-perfect conditions.

Recent findings suggest that those conditions matter for an optical ground station. One challenge is tracking. A radio communications link spreads its signal over a patch hundreds of kilometers wide, whereas a laser from low Earth orbit might illuminate a patch less than twenty meters across. As a spacecraft hurtles overhead at more than seven kilometers per second, keeping a beam thousands of times narrower locked onto a receiving telescope is far harder than hitting a radio dish.

Fraser takes a question about space-based laser communication.

Another obstacle that radio frequency signals donât have to worry about is airplane interference. Ground stations must automatically shut off their uplink lasers if an airplane passes overhead, so as not to blind the pilots (or the planeâs sensors) with a highly concentrated light beam. While each plane overflight is relatively brief, it can cause consistent disruption which isnât a problem for radio communications frameworks.

In a recent development, the real challenge though is the atmosphere. Anyone that looks up at the sky on a cloudless night can see the stars twinkling. That is caused by swirling pockets of warm and cold air in our atmosphere, and in addition to making the stars seem to dance, it also distorts incoming laser light. To correct for this in optical communication systems, engineers have to use fast-moving deformable mirrors in systems called adaptive optics, or specialized light-sorting microchips. Neither option is cheap.

Industry observers note that but the real difficulty in the atmosphere for optical communications is simple to explain â clouds. No laser in the optical or near-infrared range can punch through thick cloud cover. So when an optical base station is covered by thick cloud cover, it is essentially impossible to communicate with, knocking out both uplinks and downlinks unless another suitable base station happens to be available.

Fraser talks about the power of adaptive optics to make the atmosphere "disappear".

According to the paper, pairing stations together does get some improvement. A single one can be expected to be available a little more than 60% of the time, but pairing two together in the American Southwest, for example, can bump that up to around 85%. According to another paper from the German Aerospace Center, setting up a network of eight separate optical stations around Australia and New Zealand drops the chance of an outage to just 0.02%.

However, base stations are expensive. Building eight stations for a single mission is economically infeasible â each station costs roughly two million dollars a year to build, staff, and operate. At that rate, delivering a single terabyte of information to a single mission, if it uses a single station, would cost somewhere between three to four thousand dollars. Scaling that up to eight stations to almost guarantee consistent coverage would mean it would cost $18K to send a single terabyte of data.

The only way that math works is by multiple satellite companies splitting the same ground network. If they could keep the ground stations busy at least half of the time, it could drop the price per terabyte into a reasonable range. To support those efforts, there is a push for standardization already in place.

Fraser answers a question about adpative optics alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that the Civil Standard (CCSDS 141.0-B / âO3Kâ) developed by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems defines hardware and handshaking specs for high-rate near-Earth links. To support that standard, the US Department of Defense also decided to get involved, introducing the US Space Development Agencyâs Optical Communications Terminal Standard, requiring interoperability across terminals no matter the supplier, which includes requirements for CCSDS communication protocols.

Industry observers note that all that being stated, according to Dr. Turyshevâs paper, there is very little likelihood that purely optical communication will supplant radio for space communication anytime soon. A better approach would be to offer a hybrid partnership between the two protocols. Lasers can serve as the âheavy-liftâ workhorses, downloading massive videos or Earth-observation imagery, and radio waves can maintain unbreakable lifeline support for steering or handling emergencies. That combined approach offers the best way to make sure astronauts and all of our critical space infrastructure stay connected, no matter the weather down here on Earth.

A Surprising Newly introduced Treatment Prevented Type 1 Diabetes in 55% of Mice

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks.
  • In a recent development, developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar.
  • The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks. In a 90-day study, 55% of mice receiving the particles through a slow-release gel remained diabetes-free.

In a recent development, developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar. The findings, published in Nature Nanotechnology, suggest that naturally occurring particles called extracellular vesicles could help preserve pancreatic function. The treatment remains experimental and has not been tested in humans.

The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences. Scientists wondered whether stem cells might produce substances capable of preventing harmful immune responses.

According to recent reports, “Nature has designed something amazing,” said senior author Song Li, a professor of bioengineering at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “If we can better understand how an embryo avoids rejection by the mother’s immune system, it could be very useful for a lot of immune-related diseases.”.

Li’s team investigated extracellular vesicles, microscopic particles that transport proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells. They compared vesicles from embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, with those from mesenchymal stem cells, which are known for their immune-regulating properties.

Experiments involving human and mouse immune cells highlighted that vesicles from pluripotent stem cells had stronger anti-inflammatory effects than those from mesenchymal stem cells.

Industry observers note that the particles also promoted the development of regulatory T cells, specialized immune cells that help prevent attacks against healthy tissue. Further analysis identified distinctive proteins, lipids, and genetic material that may contribute to these effects.

To test whether the vesicles could protect against diabetes, the researchers transferred immune cells capable of attacking insulin-producing pancreatic cells into mice, then treated the animals with iPSC-derived vesicles.

Recent findings suggest that because extracellular vesicles quickly disappear from injection sites, the researchers developed an injectable hydrogel that gradually releases them over several days. The treatment was administered beneath the skin near the neck, allowing the particles to interact with immune cells in nearby lymph nodes.

Those immune cells could then circulate throughout the body, potentially reducing attacks on pancreatic tissue.

In a recent development, two treatments with the vesicles, either alone or in the hydrogel, significantly delayed diabetes onset compared with untreated mice. After 90 days, 55% of mice receiving the hydrogel formulation remained diabetes-free. They also had more regulatory T cells in their lymph nodes and retained more insulin-producing pancreatic tissue.

It has been revealed that “One thing that surprised us was that a local injection could provide protection throughout the body,” Li said. “That’s the beauty of this approach.”.

It has been revealed that producing enough extracellular vesicles for future therapies presents a major challenge. To address this, researchers grew stem cells in three-dimensional clusters suspended in gently moving liquid instead of on flat laboratory surfaces.

The method increased vesicle production 3.4-fold per million cells while preserving crucial particle characteristics. Because iPSCs can multiply extensively in the laboratory, they could provide a more reliable source of therapeutic vesicles than adult stem cells.

According to recent reports, the treatment may be most effective during the early stages of type 1 diabetes, when some insulin-producing cells remain functional. Suppressing the immune attack could help preserve these cells and maintain natural insulin production.

“In the early stages, you still have some pancreatic cells left,” Li remarked. “If you can regulate the immune cells, you may be able to keep the remaining cells functional.”.

It has been revealed that for patients who have already lost most of these cells, immune regulation alone would not restore insulin production. However, the approach might help protect transplanted insulin-producing cells from rejection.

Researchers plan to evaluate the treatment in larger animal models, investigate dosing and long-term effectiveness, and determine whether it could weaken defenses against infection. The findings may also inform future treatments for other autoimmune diseases and strategies to protect transplanted cells.

Reference: “Pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles for systemic immune modulation in diabetes therapy” by Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi, Yutong Wu, Graciel Diamante, Jenny Cheng, Soomin Park, Xiao Han, Fatemeh Sadat Majedi, Li Yang, Olivia Wang, In Sook Ahn, Cade M. Matherne, Jia Fan, Jianyi Zhang, Xiaojun Lance Lian, Zhen Gu, Manish J. Butte, Reza Ardehali, Peter C. Butler, Tony Ye Hu, Louis-S. Bouchard, Xia Yang and Song Li, 18 November 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02320-z.

The research was supported by the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, the National Institutes of Health, a UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Innovation Award and Breakthrough T1D.

The therapeutic concept described in this study is covered by a patent application filed by the UCLA Technology Development Group on behalf of the Regents of the University of California, with Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi and Li listed as co-inventors.

One Tiny Protein Change Could Help Explain Severe Childhood Epilepsy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.
  • A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to upcoming research from the University of Liverpool.
  • The study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.

A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to upcoming research from the University of Liverpool. The discovery suggests that some neurological disorders may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed.

The study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function. Mutations in the gene that produces this protein cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a rare genetic condition characterized by severe seizures beginning in infancy and significant developmental difficulties. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 40,000 to 60,000 live births worldwide.

Despite years of research into CDKL5, scientists have struggled to understand how the protein is organized within nerve cells and why certain mutations have such devastating neurological consequences.

A research team led by Ben Goult, Professor of Mechanistic Cell Biology at the University of Liverpool, identified a previously unknown molecular docking mechanism that anchors CDKL5 to the structural framework of synapses, the specialized junctions through which nerve cells communicate.

Disrupting this anchoring mechanism altered the organization of nerve cells. The researchers also discovered that even a remarkably small modification to the protein could interfere with its positioning.

Dr. Yasumi Otani, first author of the study and former PhD student in the Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, said: “What was particularly striking was that changing just a single amino acid at the very end of CDKL5 was enough to dramatically alter its localization in nerve cells. This reveals just how critical the final residues of the protein are for keeping CDKL5 in the right place at synapses.”.

The researchers also uncovered an unexpected connection between CDKL5 and the mechanical forces generated within cells. CDKL5 binds directly to talin, a protein capable of changing its shape in response to physical forces.

In experiments using cultured cells, interfering with this molecular interaction or reducing the forces produced by the cells changed the distribution of CDKL5. The findings suggest that cellular mechanics may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions.

Sources indicate that many genetic mutations associated with CDD produce shortened versions of the CDKL5 protein that lack the newly identified docking sequence. These mutations may therefore disrupt neurological function partly by preventing CDKL5 from reaching its intended location, rather than solely by impairing its enzymatic activity.

Professor Ben Goult remarked: “Much of the research into CDKL5 deficiency disorder has focused on the activity of the enzyme itself. Our work highlights another potentially crucial factor: where that activity takes place. By identifying the molecular interactions that position CDKL5, we can begin to understand how the protein is organized within synapses and why disrupting this organization might interfere with communication between nerve cells.”.

The research, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Helsinki in Finland, establishes a molecular framework for investigating how defective protein positioning contributes to CDD. It also opens a potential avenue for therapeutic research, although whether restoring CDKL5 localization could improve neurological function remains unknown.

It has been revealed that andreas Borg, founder of CURE5, a parent-led foundation dedicated to finding a cure for CDKL5 deficiency disorder, said: “Seeing how profoundly CDKL5 loss affects so many systems in the body also gives us hope that new opportunities for therapeutic intervention remain to be discovered. The new understanding of the protein’s location and function identified in this work opens up one such possibility. As parents, even the smallest improvements in our children’s lives mean the world.”.

According to recent reports, reference: “Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions” by Yasumi Otani, Emily Goodall, Vignesh Srinivasan, Neil J. Ball, Samuel F. H. Barnett, Youlim Hwang, Dominic P. Byrne, Tobias Zech, Juha Saarikangas and Benjamin T. Goult, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3338.

  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the latest Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

Recent findings suggest that at every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

In a recent development, trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine stated it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he mentioned Tuesday.

According to recent reports, "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, stated Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the fresh Congress, noted on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his newly introduced White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine mentioned congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat stated. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

It has been revealed that “Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Members of House Republicans’ newly introduced leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader highlights that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up.".

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”.

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, remarked Republicans should heed one massive takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”.

UK-Built X-Ray Telescope Ready For Action at Mercury

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first of its kind instrument demonstrates its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.
  • The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument.
  • A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first of its kind instrument demonstrates its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.

The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument.

A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Located on the Mercury Planetary Orbiter segment of the BepiColombo spacecraft stack, UK-built MIXS is the first x-ray instrument on an interplanetary spacecraft, and UK Space Agencyâs instrument contribution to the mission.

The image shows the Crab Nebula (Messier 1) in x-ray light. Located 6,500 light-years distant, âThe Crabâ is a prominent x-ray source, located 6,500 light-years distant in the constellation of Taurus the Bull. The Crab Nebula made a fine target for calibration and testing. Itâs rare for an interplanetary mission to deliberately image a deep-sky object, though they do occasionally turn up in star-tracker navigation frames.

Recent findings suggest that MIXS image of the Crab Nebula (inset) overlaid on a visible light background. Credit:ESA/University of Leicester/NASA/GSFC.

New Horizons once captured the âWishing Wellâ open cluster NGC 3532 using its LORRI imager.

âX-rays cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere to the ground so all X-ray telescopes must be in space,â Adam Fox (MIXS Operations Scientist) told Universe Today. âX-rays can only be reflected to a focus at very shallow angles, which means conventional X-ray telescopes must have very long focal lengths (~10 meters) with nested mirrors, meaning a mass of hundreds of kilograms.â.

âMIXS uses novel X-ray optics called micro-pore optics which have millions of tiny pores (20 microns wide) to allow an X-ray telescope which is 1 meter in length and weighs only 11 kilograms, making it small and light enough to be flown to Mercury.â.

Sources indicate that the MIXS instrument had to wait through 8-long years of space travel, until the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) was jettisoned from the stack joined to the Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) and the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) this past September 3rd. This finally exposed MIXS to space, allowing the team an opportunity to calibrate and test the instrument prior to arrival.

The BepiColombo spacecraft stack prior to launch. Credit: ESA.

âUntil early September, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) which carries MIXS was attached to the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) which provided power and propulsion during BepiColombo's 8 year cruise to Mercury,â indicates Fox. âDuring this time, MIXS' view was directly blocked by the transfer module, only following this separation has MIXS had a view of deep space for the first time. MIXS has been switched on periodically during cruise for checkouts of instrument health during which only the behavior of the detectors within could be monitored.â.

The image is the result of 55 platform slews over the course of 39 hours on September 11 and 12th shortly after MTM disposal.

According to recent reports, MIXS is designed to create a surface map showing the atomic makeup of Mercury at an unprecedented scale. Working in tandem with the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), MIXS will look at fluorescence of surface material created as a result of high energy solar x-rays impacting the surface. MIXS will also document the local environment in x-rays and magnetospheric interaction on the nighttime side of the planet.

Recent findings suggest that the MIXS instrument prior to launch. Credit: University of Leicester.

âThe scientific advantage from having an X-ray telescope at Mercury is that (the) surface emits X-rays when hit by Solar X-rays or particles from the magnetosphere,â Alec McCrea (University of Leicester) told Universe Today. âThese X-rays have characteristic energies corresponding to certain elements which can tell you what the surface is made of. An X-ray telescope can achieve this at a much higher resolution than achieved on previous missions due to both its smaller FOV and imaging capabilities.â.

The arrival for the BepiColombo mission at Mercury occurred late last week on November 21st, when Mercury finally captured the attached MMO and MPO pair into an initial elliptical orbit, after a close 635 kilometer pass above the surface of the planet.

This marked a first a âweak stability captureâ for a planetary mission, as BepiColombo moved inside the gravitational influence of Mercury. The thruster fire was also a first for the spacecraft stack post transfer module separation in September.

According to recent reports, there was a bit of drama last week as Estrack controllers noted the mission briefly entered safe mode and the planned thruster burn ended prematurely. The spacecraft still achieved 77% of the expected velocity change, enough to enter orbit. BepiColombo is now in a 75 hour orbit around Mercury, versus the original planned 58 hour orbit.

This comes after one Earth, two Venus and six flybys past Mercury needed to enter capture and orbit around the innermost world. The arrival was also extended from December 2025 to this month, due to an concern with the thrusters on the MTM. This is JAXAâs and ESAâs first mission to Mercury, and only the second to orbit the innermost world since NASAâs Messenger mission ended operations on April 30, 2015, becoming the first human-made object to impact Mercury.

The first mission to see Mercury closeup was NASAâs Mariner 10 on 1974.

The timeline for BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury. Credit: ESA.

Next comes the release of JAXAâs MMO (Mio) orbiter on December 9-10th, followed by the sun-shield ejection on December 16th. MPO will then settle down into a 480 by 1500 kilometer orbit early next year on March 10th, after which science operations can finally begin on April 6th. BepiColombo is expected to operate around Mercury until the end of the nominal mission in April 2028, with a possible extension until December 2029.

In a recent development, âDevelopment of such instruments is active. For planetary X-ray fluorescence, a MIXS-like instrument is applicable to many airless bodies in the solar system and would be tailored as such,â claims Fox. âMicropore optic X-ray telescopes though have since been flown on several astrophysics missions, including SMILE, Einstein Probe and the (Space Variable Objects Monitor) SVOM.â.

If youâre up early this week, you can spot Mercury and wave at BepiColombo as well. The planet just passed greatest elongation west of the Sun this past weekend, and sits just below brilliant Venus at dawn.

Itâll be exciting to see what results BepiColombo and MIXS produce as they get down to work in 2027.
