#100157. Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1319 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.
  • You can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one.
  • It has been revealed that some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.

You can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one. In a new experiment, that difference revealed up in the brain about a third of a second after each picture appeared.

It has been revealed that some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized. Those cells sit in the amygdala, a structure better known for fear.

Jiayang Xiao and Ueli Rutishauser of Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles led the work.

They collaborated with colleagues at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, Toronto Western Hospital, and the University of Toronto.

It has been revealed that everyone in the study had drug-resistant epilepsy and was already wired with electrodes, so surgeons could find where the seizures start. The memory test was a run of photographs on a screen, not anything from daily life.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” noted Rutishauser, who directs the Center for Neural Science and Medicine at Cedars-Sinai.

“Such episodic autobiographical memories, such as where we parked our car or how we spent a recent family vacation, are critical to navigating everyday life and a sense of who we are.”.

The amygdala’s reputation comes from fear and feeling. People with damage on both sides of it remember emotional material poorly.

Brain scans going back to the 1990s found that the harder the amygdala worked while someone studied an emotional picture, the better that person held onto it.

Industry observers note that so the working explanation was feeling. A strong reaction marks a moment as worth keeping, and the amygdala supplies the reaction.

Sources indicate that xiao’s team asked something narrower. Instead of the amygdala’s overall activity, they tracked single neurons that each answer to one kind of thing.

In a recent development, one cell fires for faces and ignores cars. Another fires for landscapes and ignores food. These are called category cells, and 40% of the amygdala neurons here were one.

The two explanations predict different things. If feeling is the mark, a jolt should lift every cell at once. If the content of the moment is the mark, only the cells tuned to that content should move.

The electrodes used for seizure monitoring carry eight hair-thin wires at the tip. That is fine enough to hear one neuron at a time.

Across 49 sessions with 42 patients, the team logged 1,871 well-isolated neurons. Of those, 575 were in the amygdala and 405 in the hippocampus, the region usually given credit for building memories.

The task was plain. Photographs from five categories – people, food, animals, cars and landscapes – came up for two seconds each, and all of them were new to the patient.

Industry observers note that ten to 30 minutes later came a test of 400 images. Half had been in the earlier run and half had never been seen.

Six buttons were available for each one. Three said new and three said old, and the button within each set said how sure the patient was. Patients got 70.3% right, against 50% for guessing.

When patients first saw the pictures, category cells in the amygdala fired more strongly for images the patients later recognized than for those they didn’t.

The effect held only when the picture belonged to the cell’s own category.

A cell tuned to faces fired more strongly for faces the patient later recognized. When the patient saw a car, that same cell’s activity gave no clue about whether the patient would recognize it later.

The difference in firing appeared about 350 milliseconds after the picture came into view and lasted until about 1,850 milliseconds.

The cells started responding to their preferred category at around 300 milliseconds, just before the first signs of which pictures patients would remember.

The effect held after researchers accounted for an online panel’s ratings of how pleasant and exciting the images were.

The ratings alone did not predict which pictures patients later recognized.

In a recent development, the first dataset also revealed a weaker hippocampal signal that emerged around 1,300 milliseconds. In sessions that recorded both regions, the amygdala’s signal was stronger.

Rutishauser told Earth.com that the amygdala finding surprised him because the region is best known for responding to emotionally charged experiences. Here, its activity predicted which neutral images patients would later recognize.

The fusiform gyrus is a patch of visual cortex where two-thirds of the neurons were category cells, the highest share anywhere in the study.

Sources indicate that it showed no such split between the pictures that were remembered and the ones that were not. Strong tuning by itself does not do this.

For the kind of memory tested here, Rutishauser said, the memory itself is stored in the hippocampus, and the amygdala works more like a controller.

“The system that produces the hot air (the heater) is separate and distinct from the controller (the thermostat),” he noted to Earth.com. “In analogy, here the amygdala would be the thermostat that controls the memory system.”.

The two regions were also in step. Slow electrical waves run through the hippocampus at around 10 cycles a second.

Amygdala cells fired more tightly in time with those waves when a picture was going to be remembered than when it was going to be forgotten.

Sources indicate that A second set of recordings, from 95 other patients and 5,744 neurons, carried the amygdala result again. The hippocampal effect did not come back in that one.

Among the pictures patients did recognize, the ones they felt sure about had drawn more firing at first sight than the ones they guessed at.

According to recent reports, the team then split each patient’s hits into two kinds of remembering. There is the vivid sort, where a person gets the moment itself back, and the vague sort, where a picture only feels familiar.

Recent findings suggest that the amygdala signal tracked the vivid kind, with a session-by-session correlation of 0.50. It highlighted no reliable link to familiarity.

The effect was also stronger in the right amygdala than in the left. The authors call that part provisional and say it needs replication.

It may follow from their choice of material, since the right side of the brain is tied to remembering pictures and the left to remembering words.

Nothing here was switched on or off. Every number is a prediction read off a recording, so what the amygdala does for a memory, as opposed to what it claims about one, is still open.

The hippocampal effect that showed up in one dataset and not the other is unsettled too.

The patients were also people with epilepsy severe enough to need brain surgery, and the electrodes went where their care required.

Amygdala tissue shrinks early in Alzheimer’s disease, and memory trouble is common in temporal lobe epilepsy.

Rutishauser said the findings are still too preliminary to guide treatment for people with memory problems.

However, he also noted that the research raises the possibility that a device designed to aid memory could target the amygdala, particularly on the right side of the brain.

One possibility is that deep brain stimulation could boost the activity of cells already responding to what a person sees.

The idea is untested. Earlier teams that stimulated the whole amygdala electrically improved recognition of neutral pictures, but none aimed at the category cells.

Rutishauser’s team is now studying how the amygdala coordinates with other brain regions and whether stimulating it can improve memory.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

#100155. The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • It has been revealed that the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • Industry observers note that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

Industry observers note that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

In a recent development, masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first substantial clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic indicates. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

It has been revealed that the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic notes. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Industry observers note that originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When water enters a crack, it can dissolve this calcium. Calcium carbonate can then crystallize inside the crack and help seal it. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

Industry observers note that the team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, indicates Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also plans to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

#100154. Breaking: Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

Breaking: Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.
  • Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.
  • But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.

Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.

But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.

As southern right whales recovered from whaling, mothers and calves gathered in three stretches of coast, while other apparently suitable areas drew few whales.

Researchers think the presence of other whales may help explain why those three areas grew so quickly.

Anne Grundlehner of the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania led the work with colleagues from the Australian Antarctic Division.

Her team used nearly five decades of aerial surveys and a photo catalog that tells individual right whales apart by the rough patches of skin on their heads.

The catalog held 501 females seen with a calf in at least two different years between 1978 and 2012. Nearly two thirds, 63.5%, had nursed in more than one of the ten areas where the whales gather.

Among all 767 whales photographed in more than one year, 82.4% were seen in more than one area.

Mothers did come back to the three busiest areas more often. A mother seen in one of those three with a calf was back with her next calf 48% of the time. In the seven smaller areas, the figure was 15%.

“The results surprised us very much,” Grundlehner remarked in an interview with Earth.com.

Right whales were long believed to memorize the bay or beach where they were nursed as newborns and to return to it again and again, she mentioned.

According to recent reports, A single-engine plane has flown the coast of Western Australia each winter since 1976. The route now runs about 1,550 miles (2,500 kilometers), from Perth to Ceduna in South Australia.

Southern right whales spend summer feeding far to the south and migrate to the coast in winter.

Mothers and calves stay in water 16 to 33 feet (5 to 10 meters) deep, close to the beach.

From 1,500 feet (450 to 500 meters) up, the crew spots almost every dark whale over the pale sand, then drops lower for a photograph.

Flights run from mid-August to mid-September, when calf numbers peak, and the annual count climbed from a handful to several hundred.

“When the whales were still a rarity along the coastline, the few whales visiting our coast seemed randomly distributed across suitable habitat. There weren’t any sites that stood out as hotspots,” Grundlehner noted.

By the mid-1980s, southern right whales were gathering in three areas that filled up much faster than the rest of the coast.

The hotspots were Bremer and Doubtful Islands Bays, the stretch from Israelite Bay to Point Culver, and the Bunda Cliffs and Head of Bight.

In one of those areas, the number of mothers with calves rose by about 30% a year during the first decade.

According to recent reports, daughters returning to their birth bays can’t account for growth that fast. The team did the arithmetic.

With every female returning to her birth area, a calf every three years and no deaths, an area’s mothers could grow by at most 9.7% a year.

Industry observers note that which areas were busy at the start didn’t predict which became busy later, either. By a statistical measure of clumping, the whales bunched up more each year until about 2000, and the pattern has held since.

“Instead, as the population grew in numbers, the female whales were more likely to select nursing grounds where there were other whales,” mentioned co-author Stuart Corney, an associate professor at the same institute.

The team’s reading is that mothers rely on a memory of past nursing sites plus the sight or sound of other whales, a pattern also proposed for humpback whales.

The three busy areas are more open and exposed than the other bays, which the authors suggest could make other whales easier to see or hear.

When only a few dozen whales reached the coast each year, there may have been no one to follow.

The whales do seem loyal to something, at a larger scale. Most repeat sightings of the same whale fell within about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of each other.

Grundlehner told Earth.com the findings imply more flexibility than researchers had assumed.

Grundlehner was asked what the findings mean for protecting nursing areas.

“This is extremely crucial for effective conservation management: it means that you should not just protect the places with the highest numbers of an animal species you are trying to protect, but all suitable habitat that is available and accessible to them,” she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that areas used by few whales today could matter more if the population grows or if climate change alters the coast, she said. The range also needs to stay connected, with nothing blocking movement between nursing sites.

Growth is not guaranteed. Since about 2015, annual numbers in every area have flattened or dipped, and the population is estimated at a tenth of its pre-whaling size.

Sources indicate that grundlehner’s team reported in a 2025 study that recovery had stalled. She told Earth.com that calf numbers from 2023 to 2026 have stayed relatively stable, about 8% below their peak around 2016 and 2017.

The team can’t rule out other explanations for why some bays filled and others didn’t.

Records from before whaling are patchy, so it’s uncertain whether the three busy areas were busy two centuries ago.

The photo catalog also stops in 2012, so the latest decade of movements hasn’t been checked whale by whale.

And a more flexible whale isn’t necessarily a safer one. A population that follows other whales, or returns to a remembered bay, may keep using a place even after conditions there change, the authors wrote.

What draws whales to a particular bay, including local conditions and human disturbance, has to be worked out.

After that, someone has to watch whether the three crowded areas hold if the population starts growing again or shrinks further.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, latest prescription data suggest.

According to recent reports, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the newly introduced study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The upcoming study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

Recent findings suggest that “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” indicates Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

According to recent reports, many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

Recent findings suggest that there are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The newly introduced study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

#100152. Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1592 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.
  • It has been revealed that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world.
  • On the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.

It has been revealed that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world. Beekeepers fight them with chemical treatments year after year.

On the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006. Beekeepers there report that the mites simply disappear.

At two sites above about 11,500 feet (3,500 meters), low oxygen pressure kept the mites’ young from maturing.

Industry observers note that A lack of oxygen had never before been shown to stop the mite from breeding. The finding could lead to new ways of controlling the pest without chemicals.

The work was led by Huoqing Zheng of Zhejiang University. Researchers at the Xizang Academy of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry Sciences in Lhasa took part. So did scientists at the University of Salford in England.

Sources indicate that infested hives were trucked to different heights in China. The high-altitude effect was then copied in hives close to sea level.

That second test was small, with five hives over 11 days. The team also hasn’t yet worked out how low oxygen stops the mites.

“For the first time, beekeepers in Tibet noticed the parasitic varroa mite mysteriously disappear from their colonies,” the authors wrote in a statement.

“We found that the low oxygen pressure on the Tibetan Plateau prevents the mites from reproducing.”.

Recent findings suggest that honey bees are the most crucial managed pollinator of farm crops. For 60 years, Varroa destructor has been a leading cause of their deaths.

A female mite enters a cell holding a bee larva about a day before the cell is sealed. Worker bees close it with a wax cap. Shut inside, the mite feeds on the larva. Her first egg is laid about 60 hours later.

The first egg always becomes a male. The next three or four become females. They mate with their brother inside the cell.

In a recent development, time in a worker bee’s cell is limited. Only the male and up to three daughters grow up before the bee emerges. Only the adult daughters can survive outside, where they live and feed on adult bees.

According to recent reports, mite populations can grow rapidly once a colony becomes infested. Viruses are also transmitted by the mites as they feed. In cooler regions this combination can kill a colony within three years.

According to recent reports, in China, hives are treated with chemicals up to five times a year. Despite these treatments, high colony losses continue to be reported. The mite has been identified as the main cause of these losses.

Recent findings suggest that beekeeping on the plateau began only recently. In 2004 a total of 30 colonies were brought up to the region. Twenty years later the number of colonies had grown to more than 12,000.

In May 2024 a total of 60 colonies were taken from a single apiary in southern China. The colonies were divided into four groups of 15 for the experiment.

Recent findings suggest that one group was moved to another site in Xishuangbanna at roughly 1,800 feet (554 meters). The remaining three groups were transported by truck to sites located at higher elevations.

Kunming lies at roughly 6,450 feet (1,966 meters) and Nyingchi lies at roughly 9,600 feet (2,928 meters).

The highest site was Lhasa at roughly 11,900 feet (3,637 meters), more than twice the elevation of Denver.

It has been revealed that A decline in mite infestation was observed only in the Lhasa group. Before the move, mites were present in 9.3% of developing bees in the colonies headed for Lhasa.

In a recent development, this proportion had decreased to 1.6% after four months and no mites were detected after one year. No treatment had been applied to these hives. Instead the offspring of the mites failed to reach adulthood.

An increase in infestation was recorded at the lower sites over the same period.

In Kunming, the proportion of infested bees increased from 2.8% to 21.8% within two months. Those colonies were also attacked by hornets.

Industry observers note that the elevation of Nyingchi proved insufficient to provide protection. Infestation there increased from 3.4% to 10.6% over four months and all colonies had died within a year.

It has been revealed that by the four-month mark, 25 of the 30 colonies at the two lowest sites had died. Mites were considered the most likely cause of these losses.

It has been revealed that in contrast, 14 of the 15 Lhasa colonies remained alive and free of mites after one year. Thirteen of these colonies survived for two years without any treatment.

To see what was going wrong, the team opened sealed cells with forceps. Each cell was checked under a flashlight, and young mites were counted in at least 218 infested cells per group.

In a recent development, mother mites in Lhasa never laid more than two eggs. A second high site, tested in 2023, showed the same thing. Those eggs seldom developed into the next stage.

Across 178 cells with older pupae at both sites, no daughter mite was on track to become a mated adult.

According to recent reports, it all happened fast. Just three days after the trucks arrived in Lhasa, mothers were laying far fewer eggs. By day six, each was laying one or two eggs that never developed.

The team also looked for other explanations. Bees keep the brood nest at a steady warmth whatever the weather.

Nests in both Lhasa and Xishuangbanna stayed at about 93°F to 94°F (34°C), and humidity was similar too.

According to recent reports, worker bees took about 21 days from egg to adult in both places, so altitude had not slowed them. The lowland colonies had been trucked as well.

Yet in Lhasa, mite breeding stayed low for months after the hives stopped moving.

That left oxygen as a possible explanation. At Lhasa’s high altitude, oxygen pressure is only about two-thirds of that at sea level.

Recent findings suggest that A second experiment was designed to test the role of oxygen directly. Low-oxygen hives were set up in Shaoxing in eastern China at about 290 feet (88 meters) above sea level.

A nitrogen-rich gas mixture was supplied from a cylinder to each of five small hives. The hives were wrapped in cling film to reduce leakage of the gas.

The flow was adjusted by hand whenever the oxygen readings moved outside the target range. The entrances were left open so that the bees could continue to forage.

Each hive was first kept on ordinary air and then switched to air with roughly Lhasa’s oxygen level. Under ordinary air the mother mites produced an average of 3.9 offspring.

Sources indicate that after 11 days under low oxygen this figure fell to 1.7. Almost none of these offspring developed beyond the egg stage.

Eleven days after their cells were sealed, the worker bees examined in both conditions had reached the newly emerged adult stage.

This fits with honey bees being known to forage as high as about 13,450 feet (4,100 meters). A similar decline in mite reproduction had been seen after six days in a 2023 trial with six hives.

Adult mites appear to tolerate low oxygen better than their offspring. In Lhasa the mother mites remained in the hives for several months although they could not reproduce.

In a recent development, an adult mite breathes through two networks of air tubes. Each network opens to the outside through a single pore. Adult females have also been reported to move air through these tubes by changing their body volume.

In a recent development, newly hatched mites have no air tubes at all. Instead they absorb oxygen through the skin until the first molt, when the tubes are formed.

Sources indicate that most young mites in Lhasa failed to develop beyond this first stage. The authors suggest that this feature may contribute to the vulnerability of the young. This explanation has not yet been tested.

It has been revealed that A similar pattern has been reported in fruit flies and in a common spider mite. In both species egg production is more sensitive to low oxygen than adult survival.

Other mechanisms may also be involved, such as the mother’s energy reserves or how cells use and sense oxygen. These possibilities are listed by the authors as questions for future work.

Moving hives to such high elevations is not practical for most beekeepers. The team therefore tested a simple and low-cost alternative.

According to recent reports, hive entrances were narrowed at night so that the breathing of the bees lowered the oxygen inside. In a pilot test this method partly reduced mite reproduction. “This physiological limit of varroa mites opens latest avenues of controlling this globally destructive pest,” the authors wrote.

All of the results so far come from hives in China. Only one kind of bee was studied, the Italian honey bee, the type most commonly kept there.

The effect has not yet been tested in other regions or with other kinds of bees.

It is also unclear whether lowland hives can stay low in oxygen long enough to stop mites safely. The bees themselves would need to remain unharmed.

Future research could test whether narrowing hive entrances keeps mite numbers down over a full season.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

Tech Report: The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • Industry observers note that the term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly crucial one.

Industry observers note that the term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

In a recent development, once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a major boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

Industry observers note that the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

It has been revealed that in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display reveals you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

Recent findings suggest that the only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

According to recent reports, its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support highlighted its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Industry observers note that ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Industry observers note that whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Recent findings suggest that several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

Recent findings suggest that while it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Recent findings suggest that there are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (vital for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

Sources indicate that it’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That noted, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

Industry observers note that the power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

Sources indicate that during testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

According to recent reports, several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

According to recent reports, this dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

Pulsar is a relatively upcoming brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

It has been revealed that true whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Industry observers note that another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

In a recent development, in addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Recent findings suggest that picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

Industry observers note that the two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, strategy on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

In a recent development, A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

According to recent reports, it’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

According to recent reports, the most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

It has been revealed that different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Recent findings suggest that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other complications in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

Recent findings suggest that they typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

Recent findings suggest that when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

Recent findings suggest that with the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Recent findings suggest that make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Sources indicate that never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will swiftly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

Sources indicate that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

It has been revealed that former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

In a recent development, dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

It has been revealed that “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, stated in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

Sources indicate that lePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

Industry observers note that “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden remarked in a social media post last week.

In a recent development, dunlap initially released his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

Industry News: Satellites measure a changing Earth with help from a laser in the Arctic

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A laser station in Svalbard tracks satellites as they pass over the Arctic, helping scientists measure changes in ice and sea level.
  • Today’s Image of the Day looks down on the west coast of Spitsbergen, where glaciers reach the sea and tan streaks cut through turquoise water.
  • According to recent reports, near the shore of one of those fjords, a research station does much of its work in the opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A laser station in Svalbard tracks satellites as they pass over the Arctic, helping scientists measure changes in ice and sea level.

Today’s Image of the Day looks down on the west coast of Spitsbergen, where glaciers reach the sea and tan streaks cut through turquoise water.

According to recent reports, near the shore of one of those fjords, a research station does much of its work in the opposite direction. It aims a laser into the sky to find out exactly where satellites are as they pass overhead.

Landsat 9 captured this view of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago on July 30, 2026.

The laser system at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory officially debuted that October.

It’s the northernmost satellite laser ranging facility in the world, a distinction that matters because of how often some satellites pass within reach.

In a recent development, imagine tracing a line around a globe that passes close to both poles. Turn the globe a little and draw another line along the same path.

Sources indicate that the two lines cross the equator far apart, but they come close together in the far north. As Earth rotates beneath a satellite in a near-polar orbit, its path over the ground follows much the same pattern.

Industry observers note that that gives Ny-Ålesund more chances to track the same satellite. NASA’s station in Greenbelt, Maryland, might catch a polar-orbiting satellite two or three times a day.

At Ny-Ålesund, a satellite on that kind of route can come within view on almost every orbit.

The Arctic station also fills a geographic gap in a network of more than 40 laser ranging stations around the world.

The station sends a short pulse of light toward a satellite equipped with special reflectors.

According to recent reports, some of that light returns to a detector on the ground. Since scientists know how fast light travels, they can convert the round-trip time to a distance.

Half the total distance traveled is the range from the station to the satellite. A series of those measurements helps researchers work out the satellite’s path.

The newly introduced system can send thousands of pulses a second, compared with tens per second for older equipment.

Its detector is sensitive enough to register a single photon, the smallest unit of light. That matters because a satellite may send back only a tiny fraction of the light that leaves the ground.

A faster laser gives the station more chances to collect those faint returns during a pass.

In a recent development, one satellite that can benefit from the Svalbard station is ICESat-2. It carries a laser of its own and points it down to measure the height of ice sheets, sea ice and other surfaces.

In that case, the satellite times light returning from Earth. At Ny-Ålesund, the station times light returning from the satellite.

The two measurements answer different questions that matter to the same mission.

To see why, imagine measuring the height of a glacier from an aircraft. Knowing the distance down to the ice gets you partway there.

Sources indicate that you also need to know the aircraft’s altitude at the moment of the measurement. The same principle applies in orbit.

A precise record of where ICESat-2 was when it made a reading helps researchers determine the height of the surface below and compare it with measurements from later passes.

Those comparisons depend on a common set of coordinates called the terrestrial reference frame.

It gives scientists a consistent way to describe where objects are on and around Earth, even as the ground itself shifts.

Laser ranging helps maintain that system, so researchers using different instruments in different parts of the world can compare measurements of things like rising seas and moving tectonic plates.

There’s also a local complication for the team in Svalbard. The observatory sits next to a bird sanctuary where access is restricted during the summer breeding season.

The station can operate remotely when staff can’t get to the site, a capability NASA can carry over to future installations.

According to recent reports, the Landsat image gives us one summer view of the fjord. Understanding how the landscape changes takes years of observations that can be lined up and compared.

From a patch of coast in that image, the Ny-Ålesund station helps make those comparisons possible, one pulse of light at a time.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, using USGS Landsat data.

A brain region known for listening helps us speak

💡 Key Takeaways

  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is vital for talking, too.
  • Industry observers note that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is vital for talking, too.

Industry observers note that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, claims neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

According to recent reports, A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, remarked in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The upcoming research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, indicates neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Recent findings suggest that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” remarked Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Industry observers note that electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Recent findings suggest that some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.
