It has been revealed that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Industry observers note that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

It has been revealed that democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., noted earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

It has been revealed that while ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the latest Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how promptly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

In a recent development, democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., mentioned Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

In a recent development, "I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks remarked. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

  • Sources indicate that mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot newly introduced multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive upcoming display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot newly introduced multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

Recent findings suggest that I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

My evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding major-screen TV market.

In a recent development, I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best upcoming mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

Recent findings suggest that RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot newly introduced display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

Recent findings suggest that when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

Industry observers note that the TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

Recent findings suggest that the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

The TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

According to recent reports, hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Industry observers note that under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor matter. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

In a recent development, feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

After skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an upgrade for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a big surprise.

It has been revealed that when it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A major reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That noted, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

Industry observers note that all of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of newly introduced content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

It has been revealed that as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

It has been revealed that in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other latest technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Sources indicate that both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most important connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

According to recent reports, wiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Sources indicate that all the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s vital to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

It has been revealed that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is crucial for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

#100130. Industry News: Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

Industry News: Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.
  • In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park.
  • Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.

In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park. They were there to rebuild a parking lot. The first scoop of the backhoe brought up pieces of fossil bone.

Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.

Park paleontologist ReBecca Hunt-Foster and her assistant followed a trail of bones through the rock until they had uncovered nine tail vertebrae and the leg and arm bones of a long-necked dinosaur, most likely Diplodocus.

Its relatives still turn up in surprising places, including the first Diplodocus ever found outside North America.

It was the first fossil excavation in that part of the historic Carnegie Quarry since 1924, the National Park Service said. In an account published this fall, Hunt-Foster described how the last bones of the tail were lying right against the old asphalt.

Industry observers note that the spot has a long history. On August 17, 1909, Earl Douglass, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, spotted eight dinosaur tailbones sticking out of a sandstone ledge in the Utah desert. “It was a beautiful sight,” he wrote in his diary.

His crews spent the next 13 years digging there and collected more than 317 metric tons of fossils and rock between 1909 and 1922, according to Hunt-Foster, much of it shipped back to Pittsburgh.

According to recent reports, the Smithsonian dug on the east side of the quarry in 1923, and the University of Utah in 1924. In 1915, President Woodrow Wilson set aside the quarry and 80 acres around it as Dinosaur National Monument.

According to recent reports, all that digging produced a lot of waste rock. It was dumped off the eastern side of the quarry, and in the 1930s, New Deal work crews cleared more debris while improving the road.

Those tailing piles later became the parking lot for the Quarry Exhibit Hall, which opened in 1958 around a wall of rock where visitors can see about 1,500 dinosaur fossils still in place.

In May 2025, the park was due to begin an $11.2 million project to upgrade roads, parking areas and overlooks along the route to the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

Because the work crossed fossil-bearing rock, the park brought on a seasonal paleontological assistant, Rudolph Hummel, to watch the construction.

The biggest worry was the parking lot. Fossils overlooked by the early excavators, or judged not worth keeping, could be sitting in the old tailings. The bone-bearing sandstone itself might also turn up.

According to recent reports, the road and the exhibit hall closed from September 8 to late October 2025. Monitoring in the parking lot began on September 10, after the asphalt cap came off.

On September 11, the team found the first identifiable bone, a vertebra from a meat-eating dinosaur, likely Allosaurus. Smaller finds followed every day as the crew dug down five feet. Construction sites have a way of turning up fossils, as a Los Angeles project revealed.

Recent findings suggest that the construction workers got caught up in it too. Many of them jumped in to search for fossils by hand rather than by backhoe alone, Hunt-Foster wrote, and one worker spent two days power-washing a section of the sandstone so it could be studied.

On September 16, after that washing was done, Hunt-Foster was documenting the exposed sandstone when she spotted a fossil bone in its cross section.

Sources indicate that it turned out to be a large limb bone plunging down into the rock. Construction in that corner of the lot was paused.

After a week of digging, the pair found a tail vertebra lying over the long bone, which they identified as a sauropod tibia. Then a second vertebra appeared, and a third, all still connected. Hummel followed them east while Hunt-Foster worked west.

Industry observers note that six more tail vertebrae turned up, along with the bones of the lower arm. By then, the team had concluded that the tail likely belonged to Diplodocus, the most abundant dinosaur in the Carnegie Quarry.

They also found a partial turtle, plenty of freshwater clams and carbonized wood lying directly under the skeleton.

By September 26, the team had reached the end of the tail. The vertebrae grew smaller toward the east, and the last one was missing its back half, cleanly sheared off and tilted up toward the old surface.

Hunt-Foster and Hummel suspect that the tip of the tail, if it was preserved at all, was plowed off when the road was first built in the late 1950s. Several of the last vertebrae were in direct contact with the asphalt from the lot’s first paving.

Photos from the visitor center’s opening on June 1, 1958, show the lot was still gravel, and it does not appear to have been paved until around 1959, she wrote.

In a recent development, all of this happened while the upcoming parking lot was being built around the dig. Dump trucks full of fill rolled past and rollers packed down the ground around them. “In a short amount of time, we were sitting in a deep trench surrounded by a fresh parking lot,” Hunt-Foster wrote.

Volunteers, a Utah Conservation Corps crew, park coworkers and construction staff helped wrap the bones in protective field jackets. The first small jacket came out on October 13. On October 17, the construction crew’s backhoe operator lifted out the rest.

In all, about 3,000 pounds of fossils and rock came out of the 2025 dig. The bones are now being cleaned and studied at the Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum in Vernal, Utah.

It has been revealed that visitors can watch the work in the museum’s fossil preparation lab. Some fossils from the excavation are also on display at the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

The parking lot is finished, and the Quarry Exhibit Hall is open daily except on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.

Recent findings suggest that the story is not over. Hunt-Foster indicates a second part of her account will cover continued excavation work in 2026 and additional discoveries.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s January 2026 announcement of the excavation, ReBecca Hunt-Foster’s article The Parking Lot Sauropod of Dinosaur National Monument: Part 1 in Park Paleontology News, and the park’s pages on Earl Douglass and the historic Carnegie Quarry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory discovered 2026 ED138, a distant dwarf planet candidate beyond Neptune whose size and shape remain unconfirmed.

A distant object named 2026 ED138 may be a dwarf planet between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers) wide, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory announced on October 27, 2026.

Archival images show that another instrument, the Dark Energy Camera, had recorded it since February 25, 2016, without anyone noticing.

The object remains a candidate because its size has been estimated, not measured.

It has been revealed that matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, found the object on the evening of October 13. He was running Rubin data collected earlier in 2026 through a search code developed with colleague Kevin Napier.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said.

“Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong,” he added.

The code first detected a cluster of ten observations on eight nights. Mario Jurić, Rubin’s solar system lead scientist at the University of Washington, then found 20 more in Rubin’s catalogs and images.

Recent findings suggest that in all, the observatory’s telescope saw the object 30 times on 20 nights between March 4 and July 11. The results were presented at a planetary science meeting in Spokane, Washington.

“It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years,” Jurić mentioned.

Industry observers note that the object is at the moment about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, or roughly 4.3 billion miles (6.9 billion kilometers). Pluto averages 39 of those units, each equal to Earth’s distance from the Sun, by NASA‘s figures.

Recent findings suggest that its orbit, which comes no closer to the Sun than about 37 astronomical units, is tilted almost 25 degrees from the solar system’s plane. The announcement suggests that gravitational interactions with Neptune disturbed the object’s original path.

Earlier surveys missed 2026 ED138 because it lies far south and near the crowded regions of the Galactic plane, the discovery paper states. In April, Rubin had already submitted observations of more than 11,000 newly introduced asteroids.

Sources indicate that given the orbit computed from Rubin data alone, an archive search service returned older candidate detections. The object appears in 45 Dark Energy Camera exposures on 14 nights, the last on April 7, 2023.

“Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look,” Jurić explained.

A century-long archival search, posted on November 2 and not yet peer-reviewed, pushes the record back further. It reports the object on 12 photographic plates taken between 1954 and 2000, plus a marginal detection on a 1937 plate.

The diameter is calculated from the object’s brightness and an assumed albedo, the fraction of sunlight its surface reflects. That albedo has not been measured.

Industry observers note that the upper end of the confirmed range requires a very dark surface, one that reflects only four percent of the light. A diameter between 380 and 600 miles (612 and 968 kilometers) is more probable, by the discoverers’ own assessment.

Pluto, Eris and Makemake, whose surfaces are rich in methane ice, reflect about 60 to 90 percent of sunlight. So bright a surface is considered less likely for 2026 ED138, although its composition is still unknown.

Industry observers note that “Thermal photometry or a stellar occultation is needed to decide between these sizes,” the authors wrote. An occultation occurs when an object passes in front of a star and briefly blocks its light.

It has been revealed that the archival study predicts 15 such events between 2027 and 2030, six of them over populated land. It also reports a tentative rotation signal with a period of 10.4 hours.

By intrinsic brightness, the object ranks ninth or tenth among known bodies beyond Neptune, depending on which measurements are compared.

Under the 2006 definition of the International Astronomical Union (IAU), a dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is not a satellite. Its own gravity must pull it into a nearly round shape, and it has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.

It has been revealed that the IAU has so far recognized five: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris. “If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said.

It has been revealed that icy bodies as large as 2026 ED138 are expected to be round, the Rubin release states. Whether this one is compact and round is less certain, its discoverers cautioned in their paper.

A 2019 study of a distant binary suggested that objects 250 to 620 miles (400 to 1,000 kilometers) wide mark a transition.

Smaller bodies stay porous, while larger ones have collapsed their internal voids under much higher pressures and temperatures.

The discovery team estimates that about three more objects this bright, and probably more, remain undiscovered away from the Galactic plane. Rubin’s ten-year survey of the southern sky began in June 2026.

The study is available as a preprint on arXiv.

Industry News: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • It has been revealed that intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

It has been revealed that intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Sources indicate that well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys states. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

Recent findings suggest that first, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

According to recent reports, since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

And the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her organization, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea notes. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Sources indicate that overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys claims. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more vital at that point in time.”.

Most of the world’s lost glacier ice comes from a tiny minority of glaciers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.
  • In a recent development, outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock.
  • It has been revealed that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.

In a recent development, outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock. Surprisingly, however, these land-based glaciers are not where most of the world’s melting ice is coming from.

It has been revealed that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf. They are the ones shedding more than half of all the glacier ice lost between 2000 and 2019.

In a recent development, those numbers come from a new global census of where glaciers end. Glaciers that end in lakes stood out most. Relative to their size, they lost ice about 57 percent faster than glaciers ending on land. The researchers don’t yet know why.

Joe Mallalieu did the work at the University of Birmingham and is now at the University of Leeds, with Nicholas Barrand of Birmingham among the co-authors.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mallalieu stated the lake result was a surprise.

“What surprised us most was how much faster glaciers ending in lakes lose ice than those ending in the ocean, relative to their size,” he stated.

The team classified all 216,502 glaciers in a standard global inventory by what their fronts touch: land, a lake, the sea, or an ice shelf.

Earlier inventories had flagged lake-ending glaciers in only three of the world’s 19 glacier regions. The team found the rest by matching glacier outlines against a satellite map of glacial lakes built from more than 250,000 Landsat scenes.

Recent findings suggest that then they combined that classification with existing global records of each glacier’s size, ice thickness, slope, flow speed and ice loss, plus the local climate. The full classification is public on Zenodo.

Industry observers note that lake-ending glaciers turned up in every one of the 19 regions. In Iceland, 65 percent of the glacier area drains to a lake, and in the southern Andes almost 40 percent does. Glaciers ending in the sea cluster in the Arctic and around Antarctica.

Glaciers that end in lakes or the sea tend to be far bigger than those ending on land. The typical lake-ending glacier covered about eight times the area of a typical land-ending one.

It was also roughly twice as thick, about 200 feet (61 meters) against 100 feet (31 meters).

Size alone explained a lot of the ice loss but not all of it. For its size, the typical lake-ending glacier lost ice equal to a layer of water about 1.6 feet (0.49 meters) deep each year.

That is roughly double the rate at land-ending and ocean-ending glaciers.

Recent findings suggest that after the team accounted for climate, elevation, slope, thickness and other factors, the gap held. Lake-ending glaciers lost about 57 percent more ice for their size than land-ending ones, and they flowed about 10 percent faster.

Ocean-ending glaciers flowed 44 percent faster than land-ending ones, yet their ice loss for their size was no higher, the authors wrote.

Lake water can remove ice from a glacier’s front in several ways. It melts the ice below the waterline, and the undercut front breaks off as icebergs.

It can also lift the front until it floats and breaks, or seep beneath the ice and reduce the friction holding it back.

Any of those would remove ice faster than melting on bare rock does. But the lake-ending glaciers in the census were also larger and flatter at their lower ends than land-ending ones.

That shape alone can slow a glacier’s adjustment to warming and keep it losing ice for longer, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that mallalieu told Earth.com that even the climate difference doesn’t account for it. “And it’s not just because they tend to be in warmer, wetter places: the difference holds even when we take climate into account,” he said.

Barrand stated the census only became possible recently. “The last decade has seen a huge increase in the global glacier and climate data available to researchers. Bringing these datasets together lets us compare how glaciers in different settings are behaving,” he said.

It has been revealed that the categories themselves are moving. Glacial lakes grew by more than 50 percent in number and area between 1990 and 2018, according to a satellite survey in Nature Climate Change.

Many glaciers that once ended on land now end in water. Across the Arctic, meanwhile, glaciers that reached the sea are retreating onto land.

Asked by Earth.com what happens to those glaciers next, Mallalieu said the two switches should have opposite effects.

Glaciers pulling back onto land are likely to slow down markedly. Glaciers newly ending in lakes are likely to speed up slightly and lose ice much faster for their size.

Industry observers note that in the long run, he noted, many lake-ending glaciers will retreat out of their lakes and end on land again. That matters for the models that project sea level rise and river flow.

Many of them don’t yet represent what happens where a glacier meets a lake, the authors wrote. Yet the glaciers that can respond this way hold more than half of the world’s glacier area.

The classification counts a glacier as lake-ending if any lake touches its front, however small the contact.

Glaciers with only a sliver of lake may behave more like land-ending ones, so the authors said the real gap between the two groups is probably larger than 57 percent.

Recent findings suggest that flow speeds were available for 84 percent of glaciers and ice-loss rates for 94 percent. Furthermore, the lake map left out Svalbard and Antarctica.

Cause is also unproven: the study shows lake-ending glaciers lose ice faster, not whether the lakes themselves are responsible.

For communities downstream, the open question is water. Mallalieu remarked the census did not assess water supplies. But in the Himalaya, where large populations rely on meltwater, glacier lakes are expanding fast, he said.

Better models of these glaciers would give those communities more reliable forecasts of their future water.

Untangling the lakes from the glacier shapes is the next task. It means measuring individual lakes, their depth, temperature and how long they persist, glacier by glacier.

Until that is done, the 57 percent is a difference the world can see and not yet explain.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

It has been revealed that massive thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” states senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a newly introduced appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Sources indicate that staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with latest parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

In a recent development, merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99.

Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham notes.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has declared a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y.
  • Chris Van Hollen unveiled Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen.
  • It has been revealed that van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has declared a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sen. Chris Van Hollen unveiled Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of Fresh York, the current Democratic leader.

It has been revealed that van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need upcoming leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”.

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our newly introduced Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer stated in a statement.

In a recent development, schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive strategy for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, mentioned in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

Recent findings suggest that “The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin stated. "The same is true in the Senate.”.

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

Industry observers note that “Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”.

It has been revealed that van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.".

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Industry observers note that van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed noted in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#100123. Hot days with weak winds could become a major problem for the power grid

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Hot days with weak winds could become a major problem for the power grid

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.
  • A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.
  • For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.

A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.

For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.

When extreme heat coincides with unusually weak winds, wind farms can generate less electricity just as demand for air conditioning rises.

A upcoming analysis of 27 climate models projects that these spells of extreme heat and weak winds will become two to eight and a half times more frequent over the world’s land by 2100.

How much more depends on how much carbon dioxide is emitted.

The models also project that the longest such spell each year could last roughly two to four times as long.

Lu Shen and colleagues at Peking University in Beijing led the work, with Meng Qu as first author.

The results are model projections, not measurements, and the range reflects both the emissions path and real disagreement among the models.

The team defined a bad day by two thresholds. The wind at 33 feet (10 meters) had to fall into the slowest 5% of warm-season days while the temperature rose into the hottest 5%.

According to recent reports, if heat and calm were unrelated, such days would be rare by chance alone. They aren’t unrelated.

Across the middle and high latitudes, hotter days tend to be calmer.

In parts of the northern high latitudes, Southeast Asia and northern Africa, the two coincided five to eight times more often than chance would predict in a NASA weather record.

Recent findings suggest that from 1980 to 2014, the average patch of land saw about 0.6 such days a year. Russia, the southeastern coasts of the United States and China, and parts of the tropics saw 1.5 to 3 days.

Along the storm tracks between 35 and 65 degrees north, the longest spells ran more than five days.

A spell that long means most of a week of weak wind in the middle of a heat wave, in some of the most densely populated regions on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that europe’s summer of 2022 is the authors’ example. Persistent heat and weak winds coincided with surging electricity demand and rising prices.

The projections come from a NASA dataset that sharpens 27 global climate models to a grid of about 15 miles (25 kilometers).

Each model was scored against its own 1980 to 2014 climate, so the thresholds for “hot” and “calm” shift with the model rather than with the real world.

The models project more days of extreme heat and unusually weak winds by 2100, with the largest increase under the highest-emissions pathway.

Under the lowest pathway, the rise levels off after mid-century.

It has been revealed that the tropics change fastest. Between 30 degrees south and 30 degrees north, the frequency rises by 188% under the lowest pathway and by 934% under the highest. The northern mid-latitudes rise by 106% and 689%.

Recent findings suggest that the spells get longer as well as more common. By 2100, the models project that the longest such spell each year could last 84% to 315% longer worldwide, depending on the emissions pathway.

The team split the increase into four causes: hotter average temperatures, slower average winds, bigger swings in both, and a tighter link between heat and calm. Warming alone accounted for most of the rise in every latitude band.

Winds change differently by region. Between 30 and 60 degrees north, average winds slow by up to 0.07 miles per hour (0.03 meters per second) a decade.

The authors tie that stilling to the Arctic warming faster than the tropics, which flattens the temperature difference that drives wind.

In the tropics, winds pick up slightly, which offsets part of the warming effect.

The jet stream matters too. The models shift the northern jet about 1.6 degrees poleward by 2100. North of roughly 50 degrees, that shift strengthens the pairing of hot days with calm ones, and south of it the pairing weakens.

Twenty-seven models disagree, sometimes widely. To shrink the spread, the team checked which models best reproduced the observed trend in these compound events from 1980 to 2014.

Eight reanalysis datasets supplied the observed trend, and the projections were weighted accordingly.

According to recent reports, the correction trimmed the projected global increase by 10% to 25% and cut the disagreement among models by 13% to 24%. The models that track history best now carry more weight, and the forecast tightens.

At the regional level it cut disagreement by 10% to 40%, raising projections for South Asia and Eastern Europe and lowering them for Southeast Asia and Upcoming Zealand.

The analysis uses daily averages, and the authors note that averaging smooths away the calmest hours, so the study likely undercounts the most extreme lulls.

The models also underestimate how tightly heat and calm are coupled in the northern high latitudes, which is where the events are most pronounced.

The stakes the authors describe are already visible. In the eastern United States, the PJM grid hit a peak load of 162.7 gigawatts during the July 2026 heat wave, close to its summer record.

India set a demand record of 270.73 gigawatts in May 2026, with outages in places. Europe’s June 2026 heat wave was linked to more than 10,000 excess deaths.

Recent findings suggest that the authors flag the hours after sunset. Solar output disappears while demand stays high, and nights are expected to warm faster than days. European minimums already exceed 68°F (20°C) on so-called tropical nights.

The authors’ answer is long-duration storage to carry daytime solar power into those evenings, more mixing of renewable sources, and above all a lower emissions path.

In their projections, the odds of a spell of extreme heat and weak winds by 2100 are four to eight times higher under the higher-emissions pathways than under the lowest one.

What the models can’t yet say is how often the calmest hours, rather than the calmest days, will coincide with the hottest ones.

Answering that would take hourly projections the downscaled dataset doesn’t provide.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • In a recent development, like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube.
  • In a recent development, now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

In a recent development, like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

In a recent development, now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

Industry observers note that roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, notes his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”.

Damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, newly introduced models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

Sources indicate that while the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain latest talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

According to recent reports, but a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, states Paul Goodrum, PhD, professor of construction engineering at the Colorado School of Mines. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he claims. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”.

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum claims: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”.

In a recent development, the shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

In a recent development, most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

According to recent reports, “For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” indicates Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”.

According to recent reports, recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the New Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

In a recent development, roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he notes, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”.

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

  • Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.
  • According to recent reports, the blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself.
  • The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.

According to recent reports, the blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself. In blood drawn from about 2,500 European men in the 1990s, researchers at Oxford measured more than 6,000 proteins instead.

The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.

In a recent development, one of the clearest differences was an immune protein those men had less of, not more. None of the proteins is ready to become a test, the team said. Most of the differences were modest, and not all of them held up in other groups of men.

Zhe Huang, a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health, part of the University of Oxford, led the work with senior authors Karl Smith-Byrne and Ruth Travis.

Sources indicate that “Prostate cancer is not one disease. Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” Huang said.

The samples came from EPIC, a European health study that recruited more than half a million people in the 1990s and stored their blood.

According to recent reports, huang’s team picked 982 men from Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom who later developed prostate cancer. They compared them with a random sample of 1,573 men from the same study, followed for a median of about 16 years.

Men who developed the disease were a median of about six years older when they gave their blood. So the analysis adjusted for age, along with body mass index, smoking, drinking and education.

The idea was to compare the blood itself, not the men’s ages.

A lab platform called SomaScan measured more than 6,400 proteins in each sample. The team asked which proteins differed years ahead of any diagnosis, and separately which differed ahead of an aggressive cancer.

Aggressive meant high grade, spread beyond the prostate, a very high PSA at diagnosis, or death from the disease, and 290 men fit that definition.

The researchers linked twelve proteins to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years after the blood draw. The clearest was GZMK, a protein made by the immune cells that recognize and destroy abnormal cells.

Men with more GZMK in their blood were less likely to be diagnosed, and the longer the gap to diagnosis, the stronger that link became.

It has been revealed that the authors offered two readings. More GZMK may mean the immune system is doing a better job of clearing early abnormal cells.

Or the men who later developed cancer may have had fewer of those cells in the blood because the cells had moved into the prostate.

In an interview with Earth.com, Huang and Smith-Byrne noted researchers generally consider prostate cancer an immunologically “cold” tumor, one that tends to draw a weak immune response.

“This raises interesting questions about the role of the immune system in the very early stages of cancer development,” they added.

Two proteins tied to inflammation, IL-17B and OSCAR, ran the other way. Higher levels went with higher long-term risk.

According to recent reports, seven proteins were linked to aggressive prostate cancer. Researchers linked one of them, ANKRD1, to every serious form of the disease examined. These included cancers that had spread and cancers that proved fatal, the authors wrote.

Another, AMIGO2, linked to aggressive disease, and most strongly to cancers that had grown beyond the prostate.

This is an adhesion molecule, part of how cells attach to their surroundings, and lab studies have tied it to the process by which tumor cells break away and travel.

FLT4, a receptor involved in growing latest blood and lymph vessels, was linked to nearly every outcome the team measured.

The strongest single protein was KLK3, which is PSA under its gene name. Higher PSA levels years earlier increased a man’s likelihood of receiving a diagnosis later.

That isn’t surprising, the authors wrote, because a high PSA reading is what sends a man for a biopsy in the first place.

In a recent development, the team also looked at 71 genes already known to drive prostate cancer when they mutate, and asked whether the proteins those genes produce showed up differently in blood. Five did.

Proteins made by three of those genes, ERBB3, KRAS and NRAS, were linked to aggressive cancers diagnosed about a decade later.

The driver-gene result was the one that surprised the two researchers most.

“These genes are well established in prostate cancer biology, so it was quite surprising to find that their circulating protein products were associated with aggressive prostate cancer,” Huang and Smith-Byrne noted.

That doesn’t mean the cancer was already there when the blood was drawn, the authors wrote. Nor is a protein level in blood proof that the gene itself has gone wrong.

Their reading is that the proteins mark early disturbances in the biological pathways to which those genes belong.

Recent findings suggest that the team checked its findings against a U.S. study of 4,284 men, 590 of whom developed prostate cancer. Only about half of the proteins had been measured there.

Two of them, KLK3 and ACP3, another prostate protein, were clearly linked to the disease there too, and two more showed the same direction of association.

Several others, including OSCAR, AMIGO2 and FLT4, were associated in opposite directions in Black and White men. The U.S. study had too few Black participants to settle which direction is real, the authors wrote.

In the U.K. Biobank, 18 of the proteins had been measured with a different technology, and the two platforms agreed poorly.

Sources indicate that none of those proteins was linked to prostate cancer there. Genetic analyses supported a handful, including AMIGO2, KLK3 and OSCAR.

The aggressive-cancer results also come from fewer men. Tumor grade was unknown for 31 percent of the cases and stage for 46 percent, and only 102 men died of the disease.

Some of the associations may be chance, the authors wrote, and the study had no information on family history.

Whether any of these blood proteins can predict a man’s prostate cancer risk better than his age and PSA already do hasn’t been tested.

Sources indicate that the findings still have to be confirmed in larger and more diverse groups of men, Huang and Smith-Byrne said. Their study also mainly looked for proteins that may help a prostate cancer develop, not proteins that could spot a cancer already there.

“Developing a blood test for early detection would require further dedicated prediction studies,” they told Earth.com.

Huang remarked measuring thousands of proteins in blood collected years early lets researchers begin to ask how men who later develop aggressive prostate cancer differ from men who don’t.

Recent findings suggest that the next step runs through a Cancer Research U.K. program on prostate cancer causes and prevention, which the team said will test whether the findings can improve prediction or prevention.

Some of the proteins may even play a causal role in how the cancer develops, the two researchers mentioned.

“If confirmed by future experimental and clinical studies, this could open up exciting opportunities for earlier prevention, potentially even through approaches such as cancer vaccines,” they stated.

Sources indicate that for now, the GZMK result is a clue rather than a tool. Men who were never diagnosed had more of an immune protein in their blood 15 years earlier. Whether measuring it would help any patient is the question still open.

The full study was published in the journal European Urology.
