An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • In a recent development, what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

In a recent development, what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she indicates. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this fresh climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

It has been revealed that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” notes Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto indicates. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

According to recent reports, el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, notes Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

According to recent reports, the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

It has been revealed that “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves states now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

Recent findings suggest that the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves claims. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves states.

Industry observers note that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Recent findings suggest that much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk problem,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report stated.

In a recent development, california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier states. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

It has been revealed that precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

It has been revealed that months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

Sources indicate that as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis states, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

According to recent reports, those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she claims. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

#100118. Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1368 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.
  • Sources indicate that by the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone.
  • A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.

Sources indicate that by the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone. The remaining bones can give investigators a rough idea of sex and age, but that age estimate can be wrong by up to 30 years. Turns out, a single tooth holds far more answers.

A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies. From that tooth alone, they worked out each person’s birth year, age at death, sex, and DNA profile.

The same tooth also showed what kind of diet the person grew up on and which drugs they had been taking.

Hisako Saitoh, an associate professor of forensic dentistry at the Institute of Science Tokyo, led the work with her doctoral student, Sayaka Yamada.

Fuyuki Tokanai of the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry at Yamagata University was also on the team. Colleagues at the University of Tokyo and Chiba University took part as well.

All 15 people were unidentified when they reached the autopsy table. Five were skeletal remains, ten were badly decomposed. Fourteen of them were later identified.

Industry observers note that “Different tissues within a tooth preserve different forensic information. By combining multiple analytical methods, we sought to obtain as many clues as possible from a single tooth,” Saitoh noted.

Bone is full of tiny channels for blood vessels and marrow. This means that soil, moisture, and microbes can get into it after death. Enamel is the hardest material in the human body, and it seals the crown of a tooth.

A thin layer called cementum wraps around the root, and this keeps outside substances away from the soft pulp inside.

Recent findings suggest that A tooth also stops changing once it has formed. Bone rebuilds itself throughout life, but enamel laid down in early childhood stays chemically the same until death.

It has been revealed that that makes a tooth a sealed record of the years when it grew. This explains why researchers have used teeth to track where a mammoth or an elephant once lived.

Earlier forensic teams had combined several of these tests, but they used several teeth per person, or a tooth plus a toenail, and the bodies hadn’t been dead for long.

Saitoh’s team wanted to know how much information one tooth could provide after a body had been lying outdoors for months or years.

Industry observers note that the team chose the lower first premolar, the tooth just behind the canine. Its crown finishes forming at about age five, so its enamel records the first years of life. It has a single root, it’s easy to pull, and the lips cover the gap it leaves.

Each tooth was washed, dried overnight, and cut lengthwise into slices about 1/25 of an inch (1 millimeter) thick, which is thinner than a dime.

Enamel from one slice went to a radiocarbon lab, and a root slice rich in cementum went to DNA testing. Dentin from the other side went to an age test, and the central slice holding the pulp went to drug screening.

In a recent development, the age test relies on a slow chemical change. Amino acids in living tissue come in a left-handed form, and over a lifetime a small share flips to the right-handed mirror image.

The team measured that share in the dentin and read the person’s age off a curve built from six other premolars of known age.

In a recent development, the birth year came from radiocarbon, but not the kind used on fossils. Nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the amount of radioactive carbon in the air. The level peaked in 1963 and has been falling ever since.

Enamel forming in a child’s mouth took up whatever level was in the air at the time, so its carbon demonstrates when it formed. Scientists have used the same spike to age a whale from its teeth.

It has been revealed that the catch is that the curve rises and then falls, so one reading usually matches two possible years. For one man, the enamel gave a birth year of either 1955 or 1979.

According to recent reports, adding the age-at-death estimate settled it. A birth in 1979 plus his estimated 58 years would put his death in 2036, so he was born in 1955. His real birth year was 1957.

It has been revealed that across the 15 people, the radiocarbon ranges included the true birth year in 14 cases. The age-at-death estimates on their own were off by about eight years on average.

Once the two tests were combined, the birth-year estimates landed within about five years of the truth, on average.

DNA from the cementum slice gave the person’s sex in all 15 cases. In 12 of them it also produced a profile with enough genetic markers to match against a relative or a database.

The same kind of DNA work has recently corrected the story of a Roman-era skeleton in England and been read from Neanderthal teeth.

The pulp slice went through a drug screen covering 251 substances, and every one of the 15 teeth contained something, even if only caffeine. In nine cases the drugs in the tooth matched at least some of what the original autopsy had found in blood or muscle.

In five cases they matched prescriptions the person was known to have been taking, including antidepressants and antipsychotics.

The tooth didn’t catch everything, however. Drugs that appeared to have been taken shortly before death highlighted up in stomach contents and muscle at autopsy but not in the tooth.

Saitoh’s team suggested that drugs move into a tooth slowly, so a tooth reflects long-term use rather than a last dose.

The fifteenth body belonged to a man who has never been definitively identified. His tooth put his birth year at either 1956 or 1976, and his dentin put his age at about 38.

The 1956 option would mean he died in 1995, long before his body was found in 2013, so the team’s answer is a man born in 1976.

According to recent reports, investigators at the moment believe he was born around 1972 and was about 41 when he died. The two readings disagree by four years, which is inside the method’s average error of about five years.

The tooth gives investigators a second, independent estimate of who he might be.

Stable carbon in the enamel added a rough picture of childhood diet. All 15 readings fit a diet built on rice and wheat rather than corn, which is consistent with a traditional Japanese diet.

The authors wrote that carbon alone can’t say where someone grew up.

Industry observers note that the errors here were larger than in earlier studies that ran each test on its own. The birth-year estimates were least accurate for people born before the fallout spike began to climb and for those born in more recent years, when the curve had flattened.

The age test usually works best on dentin from the center of the tooth. Here the center was needed for the drug screen. Instead, the team used dentin from the outer part, and that may have cost some accuracy.

One tooth also produced radiocarbon dates between the 600s and 800s AD, centuries before the woman could have been born.

That sample had the highest carbon content of the set, and the authors suspect carbon from outside the body had got into the enamel.

The team’s next step is more cases, and a closer look at exactly where in a tooth each slice should come from.

“Moving forward, we aim to further improve the accuracy and reproducibility of each biochemical analytical method demonstrated in this study and establish standardized methods that can be widely applied in routine forensic medical and dental practice,” Saitoh said.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that in the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

Some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

Recent findings suggest that in a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

At a similar tech giant, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Industry observers note that today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

Industry observers note that for some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

According to recent reports, cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might plan to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

Sources indicate that it works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

Industry observers note that “Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

It has been revealed that the Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

At Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The manufacturer also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment initiative. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

It has been revealed that there’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

It has been revealed that and today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious matter in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

#100116. Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.
  • Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.
  • Industry observers note that archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.

Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.

Industry observers note that archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time. This is mainly due to the fact that the same styles of tools and carvings show up across the entire continent. Even so, DNA from Ice Age samples has mostly supported the isolated view.

A woman who died around 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France has changed that.

Most of her ancestry came from the western European people of her time. However, part of it also came from populations related to central and eastern Europe. The mixing happened roughly 32,500 to 31,500 years ago.

The analysis of her DNA now gives the oldest set of genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna‘s Department of Evolutionary Anthropology led the work. Their co-authors include researchers at Harvard Medical School, the University of Cantabria and the University of New Mexico.

In a recent development, the study rests on DNA from three new Ice Age individuals and one sample of cave sediment. Thus, the picture it draws is built from very few people.

Industry observers note that the bone fragment of the woman was recovered from Isturitz Cave in the Basque Country, western Pyrenees. Excavators dug it up in the 1950s, and it stayed in a Paris institute for over 60 years. Then, in 2013, Pinhasi took a sample from it for DNA analysis.

It has been revealed that the team recovered more than 454,000 of the genetic markers it was looking for. This represents one of the richest Gravettian datasets yet.

Recent findings suggest that gravettian is the name for the culture that spread across Europe during the onset of the last Ice Age, between about 34,000 and 25,000 years ago. This culture is known for its shared tool styles, burial practices and portable art.

Until now, DNA data from this Ice Age period in Europe sorted into two stable groups, a western one and a central-eastern one, with little sign of contact between them.

The Isturitz woman belongs mostly to the western group. But several tests also found a share of her ancestry related to the ancestors of people buried at Dolní Věstonice in what is now the Czech Republic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gelabert stated the find overturned a long-held assumption.

“Until this new genomic data, we assumed that the people in Southwestern Europe were quite the same for more than 20,000 years,” he said.

The newly introduced data, he mentioned, point to population movements that were probably continental in scale, and that the team doesn’t yet clearly understand.

Isturitz is one of the richest Ice Age sites in southern Europe, with an unusual number of carved objects and signs of repeated, intensive occupation.

According to recent reports, archaeologists have long argued that it was a gathering place where different groups met to hunt, trade, socialize and find partners. The cave lies at the natural passage between the rest of Europe and the Iberian Peninsula.

Recent findings suggest that the woman isn’t alone. When the team reanalyzed a previously published genome from Ormesson, near Paris, dated to about 31,800 to 30,000 years ago, it found a similar eastern signal.

In addition, Belgian individuals from Goyet Cave, about 28,000 to 26,000 years old, were already known to carry mixed ancestry.

Two explanations are possible, the authors wrote. People from the east may have moved west during the Gravettian itself. Or the eastern-looking ancestry may be an older component, already in western Europe before 35,000 years ago.

Sources indicate that the team favors the first. The DNA signal is absent from earlier Ice Age genomes in the same region, and it vanishes from southwestern Europe after 30,000 years ago.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team took two pinches of sediment, 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) each.

Industry observers note that they came from a layer dated to about 22,100 to 21,700 years ago, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, when human remains are extremely rare. No bone or tooth was needed, only the dirt that people had walked on.

In a recent development, the researchers built nine DNA libraries from those two extracts and sequenced them 101 times. Out of roughly a billion DNA fragments, more than 294,000 were human.

After the team kept only fragments showing the chemical damage of real ancient DNA, 14,737 genetic markers remained, enough to read the ancestry of the people who used the cave.

The sediment’s ancestry matched the western group, the Isturitz woman’s lineage, so that ancestry persisted in the region through the coldest millennia.

“Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” Pinhasi said. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”.

Industry observers note that gelabert told Earth.com the team had recovered DNA from this cave’s sediment before. “What surprised us this time is that the quality is unmatched,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that he described the sample as one of the richest sources of human DNA ever reported. For the first time in the region’s Upper Paleolithic, he said, it let the team tie a culture to a group of people.

The third newly introduced genome came from Ostuni Cave in southern Italy and belongs to a male fetus about 27,800 to 27,400 years old.

According to recent reports, the team identified him as a first-degree relative of a woman from the same cave whose genome was already published. He was most likely her son.

It has been revealed that comparing the two indicated that his father came from the same population as his mother, as far as the data can tell. Yet the parents were not close relatives.

The boy’s genome carried no long stretches of identical DNA from both parents, and the population he came from was genetically larger than any other Gravettian group measured so far.

Gelabert stated this is the first mother-and-fetus pair of genomes from the European Paleolithic, and that comparing them is what indicated how genetically diverse her population was.

All three individuals, and the people in the El Mirón sediment, are predicted to have had dark skin, dark hair and brown eyes. That was the usual pattern for Europeans of that era.

The whole Gravettian, Solutrean and Epigravettian record, three Ice Age cultures, rests on genome-wide data from fewer than 50 people. This study adds an extra three.

The third is a tooth from Chufín Cave in Cantabria, dated to about 26,000 years ago. It was so degraded that it yielded fewer than 20,000 markers, enough to place it in the western group and little more.

Recent findings suggest that sediment has its own limits. The DNA in it comes from several people mixed together, and the team’s reading suggests more of them were male than female. The date for the east-west mixing also assumes it happened in a single pulse.

The study does not settle where the eastern ancestry came from. The authors wrote that no particular central European group stands out as the source, and that no genome from the earlier Aurignacian culture exists for southwestern Europe to compare against.

The team did find one thing the data argue against. Earlier work on tooth shapes had suggested a population turnover in western Europe around 28,000 years ago.

The newly introduced genomes, the sediment and the reanalyzed published data instead show the same western ancestry in place from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Gelabert returned to the sediment.

Industry observers note that “Next step is clearly to find out when the population movements that we see in Isturitz really happened. Sediment will be key for this goal,” he mentioned.

The authors named a target: the Aurignacian layers of Isturitz itself, deposits older than the woman, which could show whether the eastern signal was already there before she was born.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Recent findings suggest that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech firm and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The Upcoming York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Sources indicate that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune mentioned, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Industry observers note that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

According to recent reports, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., noted at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

In a recent development, “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

It has been revealed that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

In a recent development, “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar noted. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar remarked that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Industry observers note that moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

According to recent reports, “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar noted. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”.

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

In a recent development, A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

Industry observers note that however, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he mentioned.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

It has been revealed that “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast stated the Huang revelations could give fresh momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the concern came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sources indicate that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

In a recent development, asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, remarked his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

In a recent development, on Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren mentioned that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

It has been revealed that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an upgrade on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

According to recent reports, savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#100113. Industry News: Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.
  • It has been revealed that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years.
  • According to recent reports, an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.

It has been revealed that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years. It is difficult, however, to work out what happens inside the brain between the time a person breathes in polluted air and the onset of memory problems.

According to recent reports, an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues. After months of breathing polluted air, laboratory mice kept their weight, groomed themselves and went about their usual activities without obvious signs of distress.

Put those same mice in a maze they had already learned to navigate, though, and something was wrong.

Changes had taken place inside their brains, even in animals that had no genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s-like disease.

Before working with mice, the team examined health records from 475,325 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2010.

The median age at enrollment was 58. Over a median follow-up period of nearly 14 years, 12,758 participants developed Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia or died of an Alzheimer’s-related cause.

The researchers wanted to know how much of the risk was associated with where people lived and how much was associated with their genes.

Higher levels of fine particle pollution were linked to dementia, even after accounting for factors such as smoking and diabetes.

People with greater inherited susceptibility also faced higher risk, although the combined association was smaller than expected if the two individual effects multiplied.

For the animal experiments, the team used air collected outdoors in Cleveland, Ohio.

The particles of interest were PM2.5, a group of airborne particles measuring about one ten-thousandth of an inch (2.5 micrometers) or less.

The samples contained a mixture of substances associated with dust and combustion, including iron, nickel and copper.

The team concentrated the particles until their levels reached roughly 10 times those measured outdoors in Cleveland. The resulting concentration was comparable to the average reported for New Delhi in 2023.

At just four weeks old, mice began breathing either this polluted air or filtered air for eight hours a day, five days a week. Among them were animals carrying five genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease.

Sixteen weeks into the experiment, the team began testing the animals’ memory.

Recent findings suggest that one test involved a circular platform with an escape hole. Over three days, the mice had repeated opportunities to learn where the hole was, followed by a two-day break before their final test.

Recent findings suggest that ordinary mice breathing polluted air had about as much difficulty finding the hole as Alzheimer’s-prone mice breathing filtered air. The genetically vulnerable mice exposed to pollution struggled the most.

Other tests revealed problems recognizing unfamiliar objects, weaker muscles in the front and back legs, and behavior consistent with increased anxiety.

Sources indicate that blood vessels in the brain have a protective barrier that limits what can pass from the blood into surrounding brain tissue. Without a properly functioning barrier, potentially harmful substances have easier access to that tissue.

To check for leaks, the team used three chemical markers, including a blue dye.

Much more of these substances escaped from blood vessels in pollution-exposed mice than in ordinary mice breathing filtered air.

Some of the leakage measurements, however, came from groups of as few as two animals.

The brains of exposed mice also contained higher levels of several chemicals involved in inflammation.

Whether the inflammation damaged blood vessels or whether other processes contributed to both problems remains unclear.

Within the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, lies a smaller area called the dentate gyrus. Fresh brain cells continue to form there after birth in mice.

Interestingly, pollution did not significantly affect how many newly introduced cells ordinary mice produced. The problem was keeping those cells alive, as fewer survived over a period of 30 days.

In mice prone to Alzheimer’s disease, both the production and survival of new cells suffered.

Pollution also disturbed the balance between two forms of a molecule called NAD, which cells depend on for energy production and processes involved in repairing damage.

Industry observers note that much of the investigation centered on microglia, the immune cells that live inside the brain. Sanjay Rajagopalan, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, co-led the work.

“By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” remarked Sanjay Rajagopalan.

It has been revealed that when the researchers compared polluted-air and filtered-air groups, they identified changes in the activity of 766 genes in ordinary mice. They also found that genetic background influenced how 2,876 genes responded to pollution.

“These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it,” Rajagopalan said.

Alzheimer’s disease is associated with the accumulation of a protein called amyloid in the brain. As the protein collects, it forms deposits known as plaques.

According to recent reports, despite examining brain tissue with two different staining methods, the team could not find these plaques in ordinary mice that had breathed polluted air. Their memory problems had developed without detectable amyloid buildup.

Andrew Pieper, a professor of translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, was also a senior author.

“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” remarked Andrew Pieper.

How much pollution each person actually breathed remains unknown. The team estimated exposure using home addresses.

In a recent development, only white participants and male mice were studied. Gene analysis involved just three mice per group.

Sources indicate that “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors,” Pieper stated.

Industry observers note that air pollution’s role in human dementia needs further investigation. But unlike inherited risk, pollution can be reduced.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation.

  • These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” notes the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Sources indicate that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih notes. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

Recent findings suggest that the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih notes—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a upcoming drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

In a recent development, interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen indicates.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Industry observers note that women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen right now has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

  • Sources indicate that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

Sources indicate that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Industry observers note that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

In a recent development, this is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so substantial and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

Industry observers note that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed swiftly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Sources indicate that alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

Rainbow trout faced a familiar virus, but tiny plastic fibers changed their chances of survival

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.
  • Microplastics come in many shapes, and a upcoming study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.
  • In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.

Microplastics come in many shapes, and a upcoming study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.

In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.

Trout that lived with round nylon particles of similar width fared no worse than fish with no plastic at all.

The fibers didn’t kill fish on their own. Without the virus, plastic of either shape made no difference to survival.

The study came from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science at William & Mary, where Meredith Evans Seeley, Robert Hale and Andrew Wargo work. Anna Mehlhorn, an undergraduate at the time, is now at Cornell.

“Not all plastics are created equal, and so that creates an opportunity to identify the worst forms of pollution and come up with solutions,” Wargo remarked.

Three years ago, the same group reported that microplastics made a trout virus deadlier. Nylon microfibers stood out: in that earlier work, fish exposed to them faced a hazard of death 6.4 times that of fish given the virus alone.

“We saw the effect with the nylon fibers and had to ask, ‘Is it the fact it’s a fiber or is it the fact that it was nylon?'” Hale said.

It has been revealed that to answer that, the team kept the material the same and changed the shape. The fibers were about 0.02 inches (500 micrometers) long and 10 micrometers wide, the kind that shed from synthetic fabric.

The powder was made of rounded nylon grains averaging 15 to 20 micrometers across, about as wide as the fibers but nowhere near as long.

Recent findings suggest that the team raised 800 juvenile rainbow trout in 40 tanks of 20 fish each. Every other day, the plastic groups got a dose of fibers or powder in their water, and the tank sat still for a day before it was flushed.

Most groups got plastic for the full eight weeks; two fiber groups got it only in the first or last four.

Halfway through, half the tanks were dosed with infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus, a major cause of losses on trout farms.

Fish started dying a few days later, and the dying largely ended within about two weeks.

According to recent reports, by the end, 39% of the trout exposed to both the virus and eight weeks of fibers were alive. In tanks that got the virus with no plastic, 56% survived, and in tanks with neither, 86% did.

In the statistical model, eight weeks of fibers raised the odds of death 2.03 times compared with no particles.

None of the other plastic treatments had a significant effect, including the round powder for eight weeks and the fibers given only before or only after the virus.

Recent findings suggest that the team also sampled tank water every few days to measure how much virus the fish were shedding. Shedding peaked three days after the virus went in and fell to undetectable levels by day 47 in every treatment.

The plastic groups did not differ, though the eight-week fiber tanks showed a trend toward the highest peaks.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that measuring shedding from groups of fish in only four tanks per treatment may have limited the study’s power. A few super-shedders could mask the rest.

Industry observers note that so the fibers did not seem to make the virus more abundant. They seemed to make the fish easier to infect.

The researchers suspect the long, stiff fibers damage protective tissue such as the gills, which they described in the university’s account as the fibers’ pokiness.

“It’s likely creating an easier path for that virus to infect that host,” Seeley said.

In a recent development, if microplastic fibers open a door for the virus, the damage has to be there before the virus arrives, and it probably has to keep up afterward. That is what the tanks revealed.

Fibers given only after infection did about as well as no plastic. Fibers given only before the virus pushed mortality up toward the chronic group’s level, but the difference was not significant.

The authors pointed to tissue damage from plastic in other animals. In seabirds, scarring from swallowed plastic has been given its own name, plasticosis. Inflammation from microplastics is also under study in fish and in human tissue.

“One of the things that was becoming clear to us is that microplastics have really significant impacts, but they’re not always lethal,” Seeley noted.

Sources indicate that the team used one high concentration of plastic, 10 milligrams per liter, to make the effect easy to see. The authors wrote that future work should test a range of doses to find the levels that matter in real water.

The fibers and the powder were also not chemically identical, since the fibers were a stiffer grade of nylon.

Industry observers note that the work was funded by the NOAA Marine Debris Program. The group is now working with a commercial trout farm to find out which microplastics turn up in working tanks and where they come from.

Trout farms use nylon line and other plastic gear that can break down into microplastics, and the particles are also common in the water where wild fish live.

Earlier work has shown that microplastics can carry microbes and change how pathogens behave.

Recent findings suggest that people are also exposed to microplastic fibers through indoor dust. The authors wrote that the results call for research into whether microplastics change the course of infectious disease in wildlife and people.

They also want to know which features of a particle, such as rigidity and length, do the damage.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you.
  • In a recent development, the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived.
  • Recent findings suggest that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you. But futurist Ray Kurzweil thinks modern medicine might be on the cusp of changing that, possibly as soon as 2029.

In a recent development, the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived. After that, he predicts, it’s possible that we’ll all start actually gaining time.

Recent findings suggest that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards. But your expected remaining years of life would go in the opposite direction, getting longer with each passing year as medical interventions improved.

It has been revealed that our earlier coverage took a closer look at that prediction and Kurzweil’s argument about how accelerating medical advances could get us there. S. Jay Olshansky, a professor emeritus of epidemiology and public health at the University of Illinois Chicago, has a less enthusiastic name for it.

“I refer to LEV as voodoo demography,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

Yet Olshansky thinks research into slowing aging could produce important benefits, too. His objection concerns the much bigger promise that those benefits will keep arriving fast enough to outrun aging itself.

Life expectancy describes a population, while lifespan is how long an individual actually lives. To determine life expectancy, researchers calculate how many people die at certain ages and come up with statistical predictions. Plenty of people will live longer, and plenty will die sooner.

It has been revealed that that distinction matters when somebody promises to add years to your life. The Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table, for instance, gives a 60-year-old man 21.79 remaining years and a 61-year-old man 21.04. Both calculations assume that 2023 death rates continue throughout the rest of their lives. They illustrate how expected remaining years generally shrink with age under fixed conditions.

Kurzweil’s prediction depends on medicine improving fast enough to beat those numbers, and to keep beating them every year. Imagine a 60-year-old who is expected to live about 22 more years. If treatments got better promptly enough, that person could turn 61 and find they now had 23 years ahead instead of fewer. That would be an impressive gain. But one year of progress wouldn’t be escape velocity. To stay ahead of aging, medicine would have to do the same thing the next year, and every year after that. Without that continuous progress, it’s just wishful thinking.

It has been revealed that olshansky wants to know what evidence would convince Kurzweil’s supporters that humanity had actually reached escape velocity. Beating one disease wouldn’t be enough. A treatment might save someone from one illness and give them more years, but another illness could still cut that life short.

Olshansky does see reason for hope in aging research. He says work underway “likely will yield reductions in the rate of biological aging.” That could mean people develop age-related illnesses later in life than they would otherwise, giving them more years in good health.

Recent findings suggest that olshansky would look at whether a treatment changed people’s chances of dying as they got older. Do illnesses show up later, and do people really survive longer? “It’s important that total mortality be the measurable endpoint,” he claims. A treatment might prevent a heart attack, but that wouldn’t protect a patient from dying later from cancer. Researchers would have to count deaths from all causes to see whether a given treatment actually bought people more time.

Sources indicate that suppose a treatment delayed several illnesses and helped recipients live longer. That could change how people planned their later years, even if medicine never caught up with aging. People could have more good years after they stopped working, and some might choose to stay on the job longer. Before making those plans, people would need to know how much longer the treatment could keep them alive and well.

For now, gains in life expectancy have been getting harder to come by. In a 2024 study in Nature Aging, Olshansky and his colleagues analyzed the death rates between 1990 and 2019 in places where people live the longest, as well as in the United States. Life expectancy was still generally growing, but the pace of that growth had slowed.

Industry observers note that olshansky explains that much of the substantial rise in life expectancy in the past came from keeping children alive and preventing mothers from dying in childbirth. Saving a child’s life can add decades to a population’s average life expectancy. But in countries where most people already live into their 70s and 80s, those gains have mostly been made. The remaining deaths happen mainly among older people, and saving an 85-year-old from one illness adds far fewer years. That’s why it’s notable to slow down aging. If researchers could slow the biological process behind many diseases of old age, life expectancy might start rising faster again. That possibility, Olshansky claims, is what makes the research worth pursuing.

If only a few people received an anti-aging treatment, the country’s life expectancy wouldn’t change, Olshansky states. To find out whether the treatment works, researchers would have to follow the people who took it and compare how long they survive with similar people who didn’t.

And the only way to confirm a promise of 20 extra years is to watch people live them. “A specific prediction of a numerical gain in either life expectancy or lifespan associated with an intervention would require an observed gain of the predicted amount,” he says. Encouraging early results could justify more research, but they couldn’t show how much time a treatment added. Scientists could have good news in 2029 and still need decades to learn how many years people actually gained.

Sources indicate that even then, one success wouldn’t mean we’d reached escape velocity. Kurzweil’s prediction needs each advance to arrive in time to add more years, then another advance to do the same, and another after that. Kurzweil has noted that people could still die even if medicine delivered the gains he predicts. Olshansky’s worry is that grand promises could overshadow the research he’s most hopeful about: work that could actually slow aging.

Recent findings suggest that slowing aging alone would give people plenty to look forward to, deadline or not: more years, and the health to enjoy them. Finding out how many years would take patience, because the people in those studies would still be busy living.
